about.p: An *idiom* is a fixed expression whose meaning you can't work out from its separate words: if your boss *hits the roof*, nobody climbs onto a building – your boss becomes very angry. Idioms make English vivid and expressive, and native speakers use them all the time in conversation, journalism and fiction.

Units i and ii explain what idioms are and how to find them in a dictionary. Units 1–30 group idioms by what they are used to talk about – health, anger, success, money, work and much more. Units 31–44 group them by the picture they come from, such as time, colour, animals, food or boats, and units 45–60 by a key word, such as *hand*, *head*, *eye*, *heart*, *line* or *ground*.

about.-: Learn each idiom as a whole, with its meaning and an example. Notes on the cards tell you when an idiom is informal, old-fashioned or mainly British.
Most idioms are fixed: you usually can't change their words. Learn them exactly, and use them sparingly – one well-chosen idiom is better than three.
Work through units i and ii first; after that you can study the units in any order.

about.tip: Notice the picture behind an idiom – *in the same boat*, *on thin ice* – because the image helps you remember both the words and the meaning.

units.sub: break the ice, a red herring, call it a day

L.p: An *idiom* is an expression whose meaning is different from the meanings of its separate words. If you *break the ice* at a party, you don't break anything – you help people relax enough to talk. A *red herring* is not a fish but something that draws attention away from the real issue, and when you *call it a day*, you stop working. Reading the whole sentence normally gives you a strong clue.

L.e: Someone told a funny story to break the ice. The missing key turned out to be a red herring. We've been painting for eight hours – let's call it a day.

L.x: We've done enough – let's *call it a day* (not *say it a day*).

L.p: Idioms come in many forms. Some are verb phrases (*spill the beans* – tell a secret), some are prepositional phrases (*in the dark* – not knowing something), and some are noun phrases (*a bone of contention* – a subject people argue about). There are similes with *as … as* or *like* (*as cool as a cucumber*), and pairs joined by *and* (*wear and tear* – damage from normal use).

L.e: Who spilled the beans about the party? I'm completely in the dark about their plans. Who does the washing-up is a constant bone of contention in our flat. She stayed as cool as a cucumber during the interview. The carpet shows a lot of wear and tear.

L.p: Most idioms are fixed – you can't change their words: you say *spill the beans*, never *spill the peas*. A few allow small changes. Many idioms are informal, so take care in formal writing, and don't use too many together: one well-chosen idiom sounds natural, but three in a row sound odd. Idioms are often used to sum up or comment on a situation: *in a nutshell* means in a few words.

L.e: In a nutshell, the plan failed. He's always acting the fool in class. I don't want to rock the boat, but I think we're making a mistake.

units.sub: key words, variations, register labels

L.p: Dictionaries usually list an idiom under its *key word* – the most important or unusual word in it. To find *a storm in a teacup* (a lot of fuss about something small), you might look under *storm* or *teacup*; if it isn't under one word, try another. A specialist dictionary of idioms lists thousands of them, with examples.

L.e: I looked up 'a storm in a teacup' and found it under 'storm'. Learner's dictionaries show idioms clearly at the end of an entry. The row about the parking space was just a storm in a teacup.

L.p: A good dictionary shows which parts of an idiom can change. Slashes show alternatives: *hit the roof/ceiling* (become very angry). Notes show whether an idiom is usually negative – *not lift a finger* means not help at all. Some idioms work only with certain subjects: news *spreads like wildfire*, but people don't.

L.e: He didn't lift a finger to help us. The rumour spread like wildfire. Dad will hit the roof when he sees the car.

L.p: Dictionaries use labels to show how an idiom is used: *informal*, *formal*, *old-fashioned*, *humorous*, *British* or *American*. *The bee's knees* (excellent) is old-fashioned, and *a ballpark figure* (a rough estimate) is mainly American. Check the label before you use an idiom in an essay or a job interview.

L.e: My grandmother thought her new car was the bee's knees. 'Over the moon' is informal, so avoid it in an academic essay. Can you give me a ballpark figure for the repairs?

units.sub: under the weather, as fit as a fiddle, on the mend

L.p: If you feel *under the weather*, you feel slightly ill. In British English you can feel *off colour* (unwell). Informally, someone who looks very ill or exhausted *looks like death warmed up*. Someone who is very seriously ill is *at death's door*, though the phrase is often used humorously about small illnesses.

L.e: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today. She's been off colour since the weekend. You look like death warmed up – go home! He thought he was at death's door, but it was only a cold.

L.x: I'm feeling a bit *under the weather* (not *under the rain*) today.

L.p: Someone very healthy is *as fit as a fiddle*, or – in old-fashioned English – *in the pink*. If you are *in good shape*, you are fit. A person who is *alive and kicking* is still active and healthy, and informally someone *full of beans* has lots of energy.

L.e: My grandfather is ninety and as fit as a fiddle. You're looking in the pink! I'm in good shape after all that cycling. The old theatre is still alive and kicking. The children were full of beans this morning.

L.p: When you start to recover, you are *on the mend*, and you are *back on your feet* when you are well again. Something that makes you feel energetic again gives you *a new lease of life* (British English). A patient *turns the corner* when their condition starts to improve after a crisis, and *pulls through* when they survive a serious illness.

L.e: She's been very ill, but she's on the mend now. He'll be back on his feet in a week or two. The operation has given her a new lease of life. The doctors say he's turned the corner. We were worried, but she pulled through.

units.sub: on cloud nine, down in the dumps, over the moon

L.p: When you are extremely happy, you are *over the moon*, *on cloud nine* or *on top of the world*. In informal British English, you can be *as happy as Larry*. Something that makes you very happy *makes your day*.

L.e: She was over the moon when she got the job. They've been on cloud nine since the wedding. I'm on top of the world today! He's as happy as Larry in his new garden. Your letter made my day.

L.x: I was *over the moon* (not *over the sun*) when I passed my test.

L.p: Informally, when you are sad you feel *down in the dumps* or look *down in the mouth*. You are *at a low ebb* when you feel weak and unhappy, and you have *a long face* when you look miserable. If you *cry your eyes out*, you cry a great deal.

L.e: He's been down in the dumps since his team lost. You look a bit down in the mouth. Why the long face? I was at a low ebb after the divorce. She cried her eyes out at the end of the film.

L.p: Something that *gets you down* makes you sad, and something that *lifts your spirits* makes you happier. You *look on the bright side* when you see the good in a bad situation. A person who *wears their heart on their sleeve* shows their feelings openly. Informally, you *have a whale of a time* when you enjoy yourself very much.

L.e: The grey weather really gets me down. A walk in the sun lifted my spirits. Look on the bright side – at least it didn't rain. He wears his heart on his sleeve. We had a whale of a time at the festival.

units.sub: hit the roof, lose your cool, see red

L.p: You *hit the roof* when you suddenly become very angry, and you *see red* when anger makes you lose control. Informally, you *lose your cool* or *blow your top*. Someone who *flies off the handle* becomes angry very suddenly, usually about something small, and in informal British English you *go spare* when you become extremely angry.

L.e: Mum hit the roof when she saw the mess. I saw red when he insulted my family. He lost his cool and started shouting. She blew her top when the bus didn't stop. Dad flies off the handle at the slightest thing. My boss will go spare if I'm late again.

L.x: When I saw the scratch on my car, I *saw red* (not *saw black*).

L.p: Something that *drives you up the wall* makes you very annoyed. A person *gets on your nerves* when they annoy you, and something *gets your back up* when it makes you angry. *The last straw* is the final small problem that makes you lose patience. In British English, you *rub someone up the wrong way* when you annoy them without meaning to.

L.e: Waiting on hold for an hour drives me up the wall. His constant whistling gets on my nerves. Her rude tone really got my back up. When he forgot my birthday again, that was the last straw. He always rubs people up the wrong way.

L.p: You *keep your cool* when you stay calm in a difficult situation. You *bite your tongue* when you stop yourself saying something angry, and you *count to ten* to give yourself time to calm down. You *let off steam* when you release anger, often through physical activity, and two people *clear the air* when they talk honestly to end bad feeling.

L.e: She kept her cool when the customer started shouting. I wanted to argue, but I bit my tongue. When you feel angry, count to ten. I go to the gym to let off steam. We had a long talk to clear the air.

units.sub: know the ropes, get the picture, the penny drops

L.p: You *know the ropes* when you know how a job or a system works, and you *learn the ropes* while you are still learning. Informally, someone who *knows their stuff* knows a lot about their subject. You know a place *like the back of your hand* when you know it extremely well. A person *in the know* has information that most people don't.

L.e: It took me a month to learn the ropes. Our new manager already knows the ropes. She really knows her stuff about wine. He knows the city like the back of his hand. Ask Jo – she's always in the know.

L.x: He knows London *like the back of his hand* (not *like the palm of his hand*).

L.p: You are *in the dark* when nobody has told you something. In informal British English, you *haven't the foggiest* when you have no idea at all. Something that is *beyond me* is too difficult for me to understand, and you *can't make head or tail of* something when you can't understand it at all. Informally, something you can't understand is *all Greek to me*.

L.e: Nobody told me – I'm completely in the dark. I haven't the foggiest where she's gone. How he passed the exam is beyond me. I can't make head or tail of these instructions. Legal language is all Greek to me.

L.p: Informally, you *get the picture* when you understand a situation, and in British English *the penny drops* when you finally understand something after a delay. You *see the light* when you suddenly realise the truth, and you *put two and two together* when you work something out from what you have seen or heard. News *sinks in* when you fully understand it.

L.e: You don't need to explain any more – I get the picture. He stared at me for a moment, then the penny dropped. After years of arguing, he finally saw the light. I saw them holding hands and put two and two together. It took a while for the news to sink in.

units.sub: see the light, at first glance, take on board

L.p: *At first glance* means when you first look at something. You *turn a blind eye* when you pretend not to notice something wrong. In British English, you *can't see the wood for the trees* when you are so involved in details that you miss the main point. Something that *catches your eye* attracts your attention.

L.e: At first glance, the house looked perfect. The teacher turned a blind eye to the talking at the back. We're so busy with details that we can't see the wood for the trees. A red dress in the window caught my eye.

L.x: *At first glance* (not *at the first glance*), the plan looked simple.

L.p: Informally, someone who *has been around* has a lot of experience of life. You *learn the hard way* when you learn from an unpleasant experience. A young, inexperienced person is *wet behind the ears* (informal), while *an old hand* has a lot of experience. You *cut your teeth on* an activity when it gives you your first experience.

L.e: She's been around – you won't fool her easily. I learned the hard way that you should always back up your work. The new manager is still wet behind the ears. He's an old hand at negotiating. She cut her teeth on a small local newspaper.

L.p: You *take* an idea *on board* when you accept it and act on it. You *take* something *into account* when you consider it, and you *take* a statement *at face value* when you accept it without questioning. You *keep an open mind* when you are ready to consider new ideas, and an experience *opens your eyes* when it makes you aware of something new.

L.e: The council has taken our suggestions on board. You need to take the cost into account. Don't take everything he says at face value. Try to keep an open mind about the new system. Working abroad really opened my eyes.

units.sub: make the grade, fall flat, go to the wall

L.p: You *make the grade* when you reach the necessary standard, and in British English you *come up trumps* when you succeed unexpectedly. A remedy *does the trick* (informal) when it works exactly as you hoped. You *hit the jackpot* when you have great success or win a lot of money, and you *make it big* when you become very successful.

L.e: Only a few young players make the grade. My little brother came up trumps with a brilliant present. A cup of strong tea should do the trick. The band hit the jackpot with their second album. She dreamed of making it big in Hollywood.

L.x: A good night's sleep should *do the trick* (not *make the trick*).

L.p: A joke or a plan *falls flat* when it fails to have the effect you wanted. A business *goes to the wall* when it fails. Informally, money or effort *goes down the drain* when it is wasted, and plans *go up in smoke* when they are destroyed. An advert or a remark *misses the mark* when it fails to achieve its aim.

L.e: His speech fell flat – nobody laughed. Many small shops have gone to the wall. All our hard work went down the drain. Their holiday plans went up in smoke when the airline collapsed. The advertising campaign missed the mark.

L.p: Informally, you *have another go* when you try again. After a plan fails, it's *back to the drawing board* – you have to start planning again. You *get back on your feet* after a setback, and you *bounce back* when you recover quickly.

L.e: I failed my driving test, but I'll have another go in May. The design didn't work, so it's back to the drawing board. After the business collapsed, it took her years to get back on her feet. The team bounced back with three wins in a row.

units.sub: in hot water, out of your depth, up against it

L.p: Informally, you are *in hot water* when you are in trouble, and *in a tight spot* or *in a fix* when you are in a difficult situation. In informal British English you are *up the creek* when you are in serious trouble. When you must choose between two bad options, you are *between a rock and a hard place*.

L.e: He's in hot water with his boss for missing the meeting. I'm in a bit of a fix – I've lost my keys. If the car breaks down out here, we'll be up the creek. I'm caught between a rock and a hard place.

L.x: He's *in hot water* (not *in warm water*) with his teacher.

L.h: B Too much to deal with

L.p: You are *out of your depth* when something is too difficult for you, and *up against it* when you face serious difficulties. You *have your work cut out* when you have a lot of hard work to do, and you *have your hands full* when you are very busy. You *bite off more than you can chew* when you try to do more than you can manage.

L.e: In the advanced class I felt completely out of my depth. The team is really up against it this season. You'll have your work cut out to finish by Friday. She has her hands full with three small children. I think I've bitten off more than I can chew.

L.p: A situation *goes from bad to worse* when it becomes even worse. An old problem *rears its ugly head* when it appears again, and things *come to a head* when they reach a crisis. Costs can *spiral out of control*. Something that makes a bad situation worse *adds insult to injury*.

L.e: Things went from bad to worse after the bank closed. The old problem of damp has reared its ugly head again. The dispute came to a head at the annual meeting. The costs of the project spiralled out of control. Then, to add insult to injury, it started to snow.

units.sub: get to the bottom of, bite the bullet, iron out the creases

L.p: You *bite the bullet* when you accept something unpleasant that you can't avoid, and in British English you *grasp the nettle* when you deal with a difficult problem bravely. You *face the music* when you accept criticism or punishment for something you did. You *take the bull by the horns* when you deal with a problem directly, and you *come to grips with* a problem when you start to understand and deal with it.

L.e: I hate the dentist, but I'll have to bite the bullet. The government must grasp the nettle of pension reform. He broke the window, so now he must face the music. She took the bull by the horns and asked for a pay rise. We're still coming to grips with the new system.

L.x: She *took the bull by the horns* (not *took the cow by the horns*).

L.p: You *get to the bottom of* a problem when you discover its real cause. You *iron out the creases* when you solve the small problems that remain. A good selection process *sorts the wheat from the chaff* – separates the useful from the useless. You *put your finger on* a problem when you identify it exactly, and you *nip* a problem *in the bud* when you stop it early.

L.e: The police are determined to get to the bottom of the mystery. We still need to iron out the creases in the plan. The first interview sorts the wheat from the chaff. Something's wrong, but I can't put my finger on it. Nip bad habits in the bud.

L.p: You *bury your head in the sand* when you refuse to think about a problem. You *sweep* a problem *under the carpet* when you try to hide it, and you *paper over the cracks* when you hide problems without solving them. Informally, you *pass the buck* when you make someone else responsible. You *cross that bridge when you come to it* when you decide not to worry about a problem until it actually happens.

L.e: Burying your head in the sand won't make your debts disappear. The council swept the complaints under the carpet. The new deal merely papers over the cracks. Managers always pass the buck when things go wrong. 'What if it rains?' 'We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.'

units.sub: call the shots, rule the roost, have the upper hand

L.p: Informally, the person who *calls the shots* makes the important decisions. Someone who *rules the roost* is in control of a group or a home. You *have the upper hand* when you have more power than someone else, and you have people *in the palm of your hand* when they will do whatever you want. A person who *pulls the strings* controls things secretly.

L.e: It's the finance director who really calls the shots. In our house, the cat rules the roost. After the second goal, the home team had the upper hand. She had the audience in the palm of her hand. Who's pulling the strings behind the scenes?

L.x: In our house, the cat *rules the roost* (not *rules the nest*).

L.p: You *lay down the law* when you tell people firmly what to do, and you *put your foot down* when you use your authority to stop something. A very strict person *rules with a rod of iron*. Informally, someone who *throws their weight around* uses their power unpleasantly. A person with *friends in high places* knows important people who can help them.

L.e: Dad laid down the law about coming home late. When the kids wanted a third ice cream, I put my foot down. The old headmaster ruled the school with a rod of iron. The new manager likes to throw his weight around. He got the job because he has friends in high places.

L.p: The person *at the helm* is in charge of an organisation, and you are *in the driving seat* when you control a situation. You *take the reins* when you take control. Informally, an important person is a *big shot*, and the most important person in a group is *top dog*.

L.e: With a new chairman at the helm, the company is doing well. After the takeover, the Americans are in the driving seat. She took the reins when her father retired. He thinks he's a big shot because he has a company car. In this office, Sarah is top dog.

units.sub: the bottom line, beside the point, by the same token

L.p: Fixed phrases help you organise an argument. *First and foremost* introduces the most important point, and *last but not least* introduces a final point that still matters. *By the same token* (formal) introduces a point that follows the same logic as the one before. *To cut a long story short* means to say it briefly.

L.e: First and foremost, we need more money. Last but not least, I'd like to thank the volunteers. If high prices hurt shoppers, then by the same token low prices must help them. To cut a long story short, we missed the plane.

L.x: *Last but not least* (not *last but not less*), thank you to our sponsors.

L.h: B Focusing on the main point

L.p: *The bottom line* is the most important fact in a situation. You *get to the point* when you say the important thing, and something *beside the point* is not relevant. *The crux of the matter* is the central problem. You *hit the nail on the head* when you describe something exactly.

L.e: Whatever the designers say, the bottom line is whether customers will buy it. Please get to the point – we haven't got all day. Whether he meant it or not is beside the point. The crux of the matter is who pays. You've hit the nail on the head.

L.p: An argument that *holds water* is logical and believable. In informal British English, you *argue the toss* when you argue about something unimportant or already decided. You *play devil's advocate* when you argue against an idea to test it. Two people are *at cross purposes* when they misunderstand each other, and a discussion that *goes round in circles* makes no progress.

L.e: His excuse doesn't hold water. There's no point arguing the toss – the decision has been made. Let me play devil's advocate for a moment. I think we've been talking at cross purposes. This discussion is going round in circles.

units.O: Write a short argument for or against a topic you care about, using at least six idioms from this unit to structure it.

units.sub: you can say that again, fair enough, no way

L.p: In informal conversation, *You can say that again!* and *Tell me about it!* show strong agreement, often about something unpleasant. *Fair enough* accepts that what someone said is reasonable. *I couldn't agree more* shows complete agreement, and *Point taken* means you accept someone's criticism.

L.e: 'This queue is ridiculous.' 'You can say that again!' 'Mondays are exhausting.' 'Tell me about it!' 'I'd rather not go tonight.' 'Fair enough.' 'We need more nurses.' 'I couldn't agree more.' 'You've been working too hard.' 'Point taken.'

L.p: Informally, *No way!* and *Not on your life!* are strong refusals, and *Over my dead body!* means you will never allow something. *You must be joking!* shows surprise and disbelief. *I wouldn't go that far* politely disagrees with a strong statement, and *I beg to differ* is a formal way of disagreeing.

L.e: 'Can I borrow your car?' 'No way!' 'Will you lend him money?' 'Not on your life!' 'Let's sell the house.' 'Over my dead body!' 'It costs £500.' 'You must be joking!' 'He's a genius.' 'I wouldn't go that far.' 'I beg to differ.'

L.x: 'Dinner costs £200.' 'You must *be joking* (not *joke*)!'

L.p: *It's up to you* means you can decide, and *Suit yourself* (informal) means do what you like, often said with slight annoyance. *Never mind* tells someone not to worry. *So far so good* means everything has gone well until now, and *That's the way the cookie crumbles* (informal) means that's life and nothing can change it.

L.e: 'Shall we eat in or out?' 'It's up to you.' 'I'm not coming.' 'Suit yourself.' 'I've broken a glass.' 'Never mind.' 'How's the new job?' 'So far so good.' 'We lost again.' 'Oh well, that's the way the cookie crumbles.'

units.sub: a pat on the back, pick holes in, give someone a hard time

L.p: You give someone *a pat on the back* when you praise them, and you *sing someone's praises* when you praise them enthusiastically. People *speak highly of* someone they respect. A show that critics love gets *rave reviews*. You *take your hat off to* someone when you admire what they have done, and you *give credit where credit's due* when you praise someone who deserves it, even if you don't like them.

L.e: You deserve a pat on the back for all your hard work. Her colleagues are always singing her praises. Everyone speaks highly of the new head teacher. The play has had rave reviews. I take my hat off to anyone who runs a marathon. I don't like him, but give credit where credit's due – he's a great chef.

L.x: You deserve *a pat on the back* (not *a pat on the shoulder*) for that.

L.p: You *pick holes in* an idea when you find faults in it, and critics *pull* a film *to pieces* when they criticise it severely. Informally, you *have a go at* someone or *give* them *a hard time* when you criticise them angrily, and someone *gets it in the neck* when they are blamed or punished severely.

L.e: The committee picked holes in my proposal. The critics pulled the film to pieces. My boss had a go at me for being late. The press are giving the manager a hard time. If we lose, the coach will get it in the neck.

L.p: Informally, you *give someone a piece of your mind* when you tell them angrily what you think, and in British English you *tear a strip off* someone. Less directly, you *damn* something *with faint praise* when you praise it so little that it sounds like criticism, or you *have a dig at* someone. You *take someone to task* when you criticise them for something they did.

L.e: I gave the plumber a piece of my mind. The coach tore a strip off the players at half-time. The review damned the book with faint praise. She keeps having a dig at my cooking. The minister was taken to task for his comments.

units.sub: a pain in the neck, a safe pair of hands, out of order

L.p: Informally, an annoying person is *a pain in the neck*, and an unpleasant one is *a nasty piece of work*. Someone who spoils other people's fun is *a wet blanket*. A person who seems kind but is really dangerous is *a wolf in sheep's clothing*, and someone *two-faced* says different things to different people.

L.e: My little brother can be a real pain in the neck. Watch out for him – he's a nasty piece of work. Don't be such a wet blanket – come to the party! The charming new manager turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing. She's so two-faced.

L.x: My brother can be *a pain in the neck* (not *a pain in the head*).

L.p: A reliable person is *a safe pair of hands*, and a very kind person *has a heart of gold*. In British English, someone completely honest is *as straight as a die*. Good, honest, ordinary people are *the salt of the earth*, and someone extremely useful is *worth their weight in gold*.

L.e: Give the project to Rachel – she's a safe pair of hands. Our neighbour has a heart of gold. You can trust him – he's as straight as a die. The farmers here are the salt of the earth. A good mechanic is worth his weight in gold.

L.p: Informally, behaviour that is *out of order* (British English) or *out of line* is unacceptable. A remark that is *below the belt* is unfair or unkind, and a joke that is *close to the bone* is so honest or rude that it may upset people. In British English, something that is not *the done thing* is not socially acceptable.

L.e: Shouting at the waiter was really out of order. You were out of line in that meeting. His comment about her weight was below the belt. Some of his jokes were a bit close to the bone. In some countries, tipping isn't the done thing.

units.sub: turn over a new leaf, keep a low profile, bury your head in the sand

L.p: You *turn over a new leaf* when you start to behave better, and you *mend your ways* when you stop behaving badly. In informal British English, you *pull your socks up* when you start working harder, and you *clean up your act* when you start behaving responsibly. You *change your tune* when you change your opinion or your behaviour.

L.e: After his arrest, he promised to turn over a new leaf. You'll have to mend your ways if you want to keep this job. You'll need to pull your socks up if you want to pass. He cleaned up his act and went back to college. He was against the plan, but he's changed his tune.

L.x: He promised to *turn over a new leaf* (not *turn over a new page*).

L.p: You *keep a low profile* when you avoid attracting attention, and informally you *keep your nose clean* when you avoid trouble. Someone who *sits on the fence* refuses to take sides. You *go with the flow* when you accept what happens without trying to change it, and you *stick your neck out* when you take a risk by saying or doing something.

L.e: After the scandal, she kept a low profile. Keep your nose clean and you'll be fine. Politicians love to sit on the fence. On holiday, I just go with the flow. I'll stick my neck out and say that we'll win.

L.p: In British English, someone who *blows their own trumpet* boasts about their achievements. A person who *has their head in the clouds* is unrealistic or not paying attention. You *play it safe* when you avoid risks, and you *play it by ear* when you decide what to do as things happen. People who *keep up with the Joneses* try to own the same things as their neighbours.

L.e: He's always blowing his own trumpet. She has her head in the clouds – she forgot the meeting again. I'll play it safe and take an umbrella. We haven't made plans – we'll play it by ear. They bought a new car just to keep up with the Joneses.

units.sub: take with a pinch of salt, take to heart, laugh off

L.p: You *take* something *with a pinch of salt* when you don't completely believe it. You *take someone at their word* when you believe what they say. Someone who believes a lie completely falls for it *hook, line and sinker* (informal). Informally, *A likely story!* is an ironic way of saying you don't believe someone, and you *smell a rat* when you suspect that something is wrong.

L.e: Take his stories with a pinch of salt – he loves to exaggerate. She said she'd pay me back, and I took her at her word. He fell for the excuse hook, line and sinker. 'I was stuck in traffic for three hours.' 'A likely story!' When the 'bank' asked for my password, I smelt a rat.

L.x: Take his stories *with a pinch of salt* (not *with a pinch of sugar*).

L.p: You *take* criticism *to heart* when you are deeply affected by it, and you *take* a remark *the wrong way* when you misunderstand it and are offended. You *laugh off* criticism when you pretend it isn't important by joking about it. Words that *hit home* make you realise an unpleasant truth, and a remark that *cuts you to the quick* hurts your feelings deeply.

L.e: My grandmother takes every comment about her cooking to heart. I hope you didn't take my comment the wrong way. She laughed off the criticism. His words really hit home. Her cruel remark cut him to the quick.

L.p: Advice that *falls on deaf ears* is ignored, and informally something that *goes in one ear and out the other* is heard but quickly forgotten. You *turn a deaf ear to* requests when you refuse to listen to them, and you *lend an ear* when you listen sympathetically. You *give someone the benefit of the doubt* when you decide to believe them although you aren't sure.

L.e: My warnings fell on deaf ears. Everything I tell him goes in one ear and out the other. The government turned a deaf ear to their complaints. She's always ready to lend an ear. His story sounded odd, but I gave him the benefit of the doubt.

units.sub: on thin ice, play with fire, a close shave

L.p: You are *on thin ice* when you are in a risky situation that could easily lead to trouble. You *play with fire* when you do something dangerous. Informally, you *push your luck* when you take another risk after already being lucky. Someone who *lives on the edge* takes a lot of risks.

L.e: You're on thin ice – one more late arrival and you'll lose your job. Borrowing money from them is playing with fire. Don't push your luck – you've already had one warning. He loves extreme sports and lives on the edge.

L.x: You're *on thin ice* (not *on thin water*) with the boss.

L.p: Informally, *a close shave* is a situation where you nearly have an accident, and *a close call* means the same. You escape *by the skin of your teeth* when you only just escape. People who have *a narrow escape* are almost hurt or killed. You are *out of the woods* when you are no longer in danger.

L.e: That was a close shave – the lorry missed us by inches! It was a close call, but nobody was hurt. She caught the last train by the skin of her teeth. They had a narrow escape when the roof collapsed. The doctors say he's not out of the woods yet.

L.p: A plan can be *a recipe for disaster* (very likely to go wrong) or a problem *a ticking time bomb* (something that will cause serious trouble later). Something that *rings alarm bells* makes people worried, and *a red flag* is a warning sign. People *sail close to the wind* when they do something that is nearly illegal or dangerous.

L.e: Mixing those two personalities is a recipe for disaster. The old wiring is a ticking time bomb. His sudden wealth rang alarm bells with the police. A job advert that asks you to pay a fee is a red flag. Their accounting methods were sailing close to the wind.

units.sub: go the extra mile, bend over backwards, by hook or by crook

L.p: You *go the extra mile* when you make more effort than is expected, and you *bend over backwards* when you try very hard to help someone. You *pull out all the stops* when you make every possible effort. Someone who *works their fingers to the bone* works extremely hard, and you *give it your all* when you try as hard as you can.

L.e: The hotel staff went the extra mile to make our stay special. My parents bent over backwards to help us move. We pulled out all the stops for her birthday. She worked her fingers to the bone to send her children to university. Win or lose, give it your all.

L.x: The staff *went the extra mile* (not *went the extra kilometre*) for us.

L.p: You do something *by hook or by crook* when you are determined to do it by any method. You *move heaven and earth* when you try everything possible, and you *leave no stone unturned* when you search everywhere or try every possibility. You *keep your nose to the grindstone* when you work hard for a long time, and informally you *stick at it* when you continue despite difficulties.

L.e: I'll get a ticket for that concert by hook or by crook. She moved heaven and earth to find her lost cat. Police left no stone unturned in their search. He kept his nose to the grindstone all year and passed. Learning the piano is hard, but stick at it.

L.p: You *rest on your laurels* when you stop trying because you are happy with past success. In informal British English, someone who *doesn't do a stroke* does no work at all. You *cut corners* when you do something badly to save time or money, and you *go through the motions* when you do something without real effort or interest. A very lazy person is *bone idle* (British English, informal).

L.e: Winning one match is no reason to rest on our laurels. He didn't do a stroke of work all weekend. The builders cut corners, and now the roof leaks. She just goes through the motions at work these days. My flatmate is bone idle.

units.sub: a necessary evil, the be-all and end-all, the last resort

L.p: A *necessary evil* is something unpleasant that you have to accept. Informally, something essential is *a must*. You say you *can't do without* something you need very much. *The bare necessities* are the most basic things you need, and something done *as a matter of course* is a normal part of a process.

L.e: For most people, commuting is a necessary evil. A good coat is a must in a Scottish winter. I couldn't do without my phone. The hostel provides only the bare necessities. Safety checks are carried out as a matter of course.

L.x: For most people, commuting is *a necessary evil* (not *a needed evil*).

L.p: *The be-all and end-all* is the most important thing in a situation, and the phrase is often used in the negative. Informally, something *to die for* is extremely good, and something that is *just what the doctor ordered* is exactly what you need. You *have your heart set on* something when you want it very much. An extra pleasure on top of an already good day is *the icing on the cake*.

L.e: Money isn't the be-all and end-all. Their chocolate cake is to die for. A week in the sun was just what the doctor ordered. She has her heart set on studying medicine. We won the match, and the sunshine was the icing on the cake.

L.p: *The last resort* is what you do only when everything else has failed. Things that are *surplus to requirements* are not needed (British English, formal or humorous). Something *neither here nor there* is not important. In informal British English, you stand around *like a spare part* when you feel useless, and something that *doesn't matter a jot* is completely unimportant.

L.e: Borrowing from my parents is the last resort. The old desks were surplus to requirements. Whether we leave at six or seven is neither here nor there. Everyone else was busy, and I stood around like a spare part. It doesn't matter a jot what they think.

units.sub: a long shot, touch wood, the odds are against

L.p: In British English, something *on the cards* is likely to happen. An attempt that is *a long shot* has only a small chance of success, and *the odds are against* something when it is unlikely. People say *Pigs might fly!* (British English, humorous) about something they think will never happen. Informally, *a dead cert* is something certain to happen.

L.e: A rise in interest rates is on the cards. Applying so late is a long shot, but it's worth a try. The odds are against them winning away from home. 'He says he'll tidy his room.' 'Pigs might fly!' She's a dead cert for the job.

L.x: It's *a long shot* (not *a far shot*), but we might still win.

L.p: Informally, you *strike it lucky* when you have good luck, and something happens *by a stroke of luck* when it happens luckily. *A lucky break* is a lucky chance that helps you succeed. People *keep their fingers crossed* when they hope for good luck, and in British English they say *touch wood* after mentioning their good fortune, to avoid bad luck. *Beginner's luck* is success when you are new to something.

L.e: We struck it lucky with the weather. By a stroke of luck, the train was late too. Her lucky break came when a director saw her in a school play. Keep your fingers crossed for me tomorrow. I've never broken a bone – touch wood! I won the first game, but it was just beginner's luck.

L.p: You *draw the short straw* when you are chosen to do an unpleasant task. In British English, a result is *in the lap of the gods* when it depends on luck. You *take your chances* when you accept a risk, and informally something is *anyone's guess* when nobody knows what will happen. Someone *down on their luck* has had a lot of bad luck.

L.e: I drew the short straw and had to work on Christmas Day. Whether we finish on time is in the lap of the gods. There's no forecast, so we'll take our chances. Who will win? It's anyone's guess. He's been down on his luck since losing his job.

units.sub: born with a silver spoon in your mouth, the upper crust, climb the social ladder

L.p: Someone *born with a silver spoon in their mouth* comes from a rich family. Informally, *the upper crust* are the highest social class. You *move in high circles* when you spend time with important people, and *the great and the good* are important, respected people – the phrase is often used ironically. Informally, people who are *well-heeled* are rich.

L.e: He was born with a silver spoon in his mouth and never had to work. The restaurant is popular with the upper crust. She moves in very high circles. The great and the good gathered for the opening of the gallery. The village has become popular with well-heeled Londoners.

L.x: He was born *with a silver spoon in his mouth* (not *with a gold spoon in his mouth*).

L.p: You *climb the social ladder* when you improve your social position. You *go up in the world* when you become richer or more important, and you *come down in the world* when you become poorer. A person who goes *from rags to riches* starts poor and becomes very rich.

L.e: She worked hard to climb the social ladder. You've gone up in the world – a company car! The family came down in the world after the war. His life is a classic rags-to-riches story.

L.p: *The man in the street* is an ordinary person, and *the haves and the have-nots* are rich people and poor people. People *keep up appearances* when they hide that they have less money than before. Someone who *looks down their nose at* others thinks they are better than them, and *a big fish in a small pond* is important only in a small place.

L.e: Ask the man in the street and he'll say prices are too high. The gap between the haves and the have-nots is growing. Despite their debts, they kept up appearances. She looks down her nose at anyone without a degree. In his village he's a big fish in a small pond.

units.sub: butterflies in your stomach, on edge, at the end of your tether

L.p: You have *butterflies in your stomach* when you feel nervous before something. You are *on edge* when you are nervous and easily upset, and *on tenterhooks* when you are anxiously waiting for news. You are *at your wits' end* when you are so worried that you don't know what to do, and – in British English – *at the end of your tether* when you have no patience left.

L.e: Walking onto the stage, the young violinist had butterflies in her stomach. Everyone was on edge waiting for the results. We were on tenterhooks all evening. I'm at my wits' end – the baby won't stop crying. By Friday I was at the end of my tether.

L.x: I had *butterflies in my stomach* (not *birds in my stomach*) before the speech.

L.p: Something *makes your blood run cold* when it frightens you very much, and a story *makes your hair stand on end* when it terrifies you. Informally, you are *scared stiff* when you are extremely frightened. In informal British English, news that *knocks you for six* shocks you badly, and you are *in a state* when you are very upset or nervous.

L.e: The scream made my blood run cold. The ghost story made my hair stand on end. I was scared stiff during the storm. The news of his illness knocked me for six. She was in a real state before the interview.

L.p: In British English, you keep *a stiff upper lip* when you hide your feelings in a difficult situation. Someone *cool, calm and collected* is relaxed and in control. Informally in British English, *Keep your hair on!* tells someone not to get angry. You *take* problems *in your stride* when you deal with them calmly, and good news *takes a weight off your mind*.

L.e: He kept a stiff upper lip throughout the funeral. She was cool, calm and collected in the final. Keep your hair on – it's only a scratch. She takes changes in her stride. Paying off the loan took a weight off my mind.

units.sub: get on like a house on fire, at loggerheads, see eye to eye

L.p: Informally, two people *get on like a house on fire* when they like each other very much, and they *hit it off* when they like each other immediately. You *see eye to eye* with someone when you agree. People *on the same wavelength* understand each other well, and informally very close friends are *as thick as thieves*.

L.e: My mum and my wife get on like a house on fire. We hit it off the moment we met. My brother and I don't always see eye to eye. We're on the same wavelength about most things. Those two are as thick as thieves.

L.x: My brother and I don't always *see eye to eye* (not *see face to face*).

L.p: People are *at loggerheads* when they disagree strongly, and two people who argue all the time *fight like cat and dog*. After a quarrel, people may be *not on speaking terms*. Informally, you *have a bone to pick with* someone when you want to complain about something they did. There is *bad blood* between people who have disliked each other for a long time.

L.e: The council and the residents are at loggerheads over the new road. My two sisters fight like cat and dog. After the wedding, the cousins weren't on speaking terms. I've got a bone to pick with you. There's been bad blood between the two families for years.

L.p: Informally, people *patch things up* when they end a quarrel, and you *make amends* when you do something to correct a wrong. You *build bridges* when you try to improve relations between people or groups. Informally, someone *pops the question* when they ask their partner to marry them, and a couple *ties the knot* when they marry.

L.e: After years of silence, the brothers patched things up. He sent flowers to make amends. The festival helps to build bridges between the two communities. He popped the question on top of a mountain. They're tying the knot in June.

units.sub: the tip of the iceberg, a drop in the ocean, in the middle of nowhere

L.p: *The tip of the iceberg* is a small, visible part of a much bigger problem. *A drop in the ocean* is an amount too small to make a difference. A person who is *larger than life* is more exciting and colourful than most people. In informal British English, a tiny room has *no room to swing a cat*, and things that are *thin on the ground* are rare.

L.e: These complaints are only the tip of the iceberg. The donation is a drop in the ocean compared with what's needed. Her uncle is a larger-than-life character. The flat is so small there's no room to swing a cat. Good plumbers are thin on the ground round here.

L.x: The money is *a drop in the ocean* (not *a drop in the sea*).

L.p: A place *in the middle of nowhere* is far from towns, and one *off the beaten track* is away from the places tourists usually visit. Someone *in the thick of* something is very involved in it, while someone *on the sidelines* is not involved. Something *under your nose* is very close to you but not noticed.

L.e: They live in a cottage in the middle of nowhere. We found a café off the beaten track. She was in the thick of the negotiations. He preferred to stay on the sidelines. My glasses were right under my nose all the time.

L.p: Someone *head and shoulders above* the others is much better than them, and something *second to none* is the best. An object with *pride of place* is in the most important or noticeable position. You *take a back seat* when you let others take control, and informally newcomers are *at the bottom of the pile*.

L.e: As a player, she's head and shoulders above the rest. The service here is second to none. The trophy has pride of place on the mantelpiece. After retiring, he took a back seat in the business. New staff are always at the bottom of the pile.

units.sub: pay through the nose, make ends meet, tighten your belt

L.p: Informally, people who are *rolling in it* are very rich, and someone with *money to burn* has more than they need. Something that *costs the earth* is very expensive. A business *makes a killing* when it makes a lot of money quickly, and you *strike it rich* when you suddenly become rich.

L.e: His family is rolling in it. Who has money to burn on a gold-plated phone? That car must have cost the earth. Ticket touts made a killing at the final. They struck it rich when oil was found on their land.

L.x: That car must have *cost the earth* (not *cost the world*).

L.h: B Paying too much or too little

L.p: Informally, you *pay through the nose* when you pay far too much, and something overpriced is *a rip-off*. Work done *on the cheap* is done as cheaply as possible. You get something *for a song* when you buy it very cheaply. In British English, a shockingly high price is *daylight robbery*.

L.e: We paid through the nose for the tickets. Fifteen pounds for a sandwich? What a rip-off! They did the repairs on the cheap, and it shows. I bought this guitar for a song at a car boot sale. Six pounds for a coffee is daylight robbery!

L.p: You *make ends meet* when you have just enough money to live on, and you *tighten your belt* when you spend less because you have less. People *on the breadline* are very poor. Families *feel the pinch* when they have less money than before, and you *save for a rainy day* when you keep money for difficult times.

L.e: With three children, they struggle to make ends meet. When the factory cut everyone's hours, the whole town had to tighten its belt. Millions of people live on the breadline. Families are feeling the pinch as prices rise. Grandma always told me to save for a rainy day.

units.sub: snowed under, a dead-end job, climb the ladder

L.p: Informally, you are *snowed under* when you have too much work, and *up to your eyes* in work when you are extremely busy. You *burn the midnight oil* when you work late into the night, and you *work all hours* when you work very long days. You *keep your head above water* when you only just manage to cope.

L.e: I'm snowed under with reports this week. She's up to her eyes in exams at the moment. I burned the midnight oil to finish the presentation. Since opening the café, they've worked all hours. With two people off sick, we're barely keeping our heads above water.

L.x: I'm *snowed under* (not *snowed over*) with work.

L.p: *A dead-end job* has no chance of promotion. You *climb the ladder* when you get better and better jobs, and you *get your foot in the door* when you get a first chance in an organisation. *A high-flyer* is very successful in their career. In informal British English, you *get the sack* when you lose your job.

L.e: He's stuck in a dead-end job at the warehouse. She climbed the ladder quickly at the bank. An internship is a good way to get your foot in the door. My sister is a high-flyer in advertising. He got the sack for being late every day.

L.p: You *pull your weight* when you do your fair share of work, and someone *on the ball* is quick to understand and react. You do things *by the book* when you follow the rules exactly, and informally you *drop the ball* when you fail to do something you should. In British English, *a busman's holiday* is time off spent doing your usual work, and a *jobsworth* (informal) follows rules so strictly that they refuse to help.

L.e: Everyone in the team has to pull their weight. Our new receptionist is really on the ball. The inspector does everything by the book. Someone dropped the ball and the order was never sent. For a chef, cooking for friends is a busman's holiday. Some jobsworth wouldn't let me in five minutes early.

units.sub: in the blink of an eye, at a snail's pace, a stone's throw

L.p: Something that happens *in the blink of an eye* happens extremely quickly. You do something *at the drop of a hat* when you do it immediately, without hesitating. Something moving *at a snail's pace* is very slow, and something done *at breakneck speed* is dangerously fast. You finish a job *in no time* when you finish it very quickly.

L.e: The holiday was over in the blink of an eye. She'd help anyone at the drop of a hat. Traffic was moving at a snail's pace. He drove at breakneck speed to the hospital. We'll have this finished in no time.

L.x: Traffic moved *at a snail's pace* (not *at a turtle's pace*) through the town.

L.p: A place *a stone's throw* away is very close, and somewhere *within easy reach* is close and easy to get to. Informally, a place *miles from anywhere* is far from towns. You *go the distance* when you continue to the end of something difficult. Two opinions that are *poles apart* are completely different.

L.e: The flat is a stone's throw from the station. The beach is within easy reach of the hotel. The farm is miles from anywhere. Few people thought the young boxer would go the distance. My parents' politics are poles apart.

L.p: Informally, you work *flat out* when you work as fast or as hard as possible. Music on *full blast* is at maximum volume. You *go all out* when you make every effort. Informally, something *over the top* is too extreme. A *full-blown* problem is fully developed, and something done *to the hilt* is done completely.

L.e: We worked flat out to finish by Friday. The neighbours had the music on full blast. The team went all out for a win. The decorations were a bit over the top. A small disagreement turned into a full-blown row. The house is mortgaged to the hilt.

units.sub: in a nutshell, a play on words, lost for words

L.h: A Commenting on what is said

L.p: You say something *in a nutshell* when you say it in very few words. *A play on words* is a joke that uses a word with two meanings, or two words that sound alike. If someone did not say something *in so many words*, they did not say it directly, but their meaning was still clear. *A turn of phrase* is a particular way of expressing something, and a nice turn of phrase is a clever or attractive one. People say *famous last words* as a joke when someone has just said something confident that will probably turn out to be wrong.

L.e: In a nutshell, we need more staff and less paperwork. The bakery is called 'Bread Expectations', which is a play on words. She didn't say it in so many words, but she wants to leave. Her letters are full of lovely turns of phrase. 'This train is never late.' Famous last words!

L.x: The bakery's name is *a play on words* (not *a game of words*).

L.h: B Talking too much or too little

L.p: If you are *lost for words*, you are so surprised, moved or shocked that you cannot think what to say. Someone who is *tongue-tied* cannot speak easily because they are nervous or shy. In British English, people who *talk nineteen to the dozen* talk very fast and without stopping. A person with *the gift of the gab* can talk easily and persuasively. If you *can't get a word in edgeways*, the other person talks so much that you have no chance to speak.

L.e: When they gave me the award, I was lost for words. I always get tongue-tied when I meet someone famous. The two sisters sat in the kitchen, talking nineteen to the dozen. With the gift of the gab like his, he should be in sales. My uncle talked all evening, and nobody could get a word in edgeways.

L.x: Her kind speech left me *lost for words* (not *lost of words*).

L.h: C Words and what they do

L.p: Someone who does *not mince their words* says exactly what they think, even if it upsets people. You have to *eat your words* when you must admit that something you said was wrong. In an argument, the person who *has the last word* makes the final comment. If someone *puts words into your mouth*, they suggest that you said or meant something that you did not. When someone *takes the words out of your mouth*, they say exactly what you were about to say.

L.e: The report does not mince its words: the hospital is failing. He said I'd never pass my driving test, but I made him eat his words. My sister always has to have the last word. Don't put words into my mouth – I never said I was unhappy. 'Shall we get a takeaway?' 'You took the words right out of my mouth!'

L.x: Critics said the film would fail, but now they're having to *eat their words* (not *swallow their words*).

units.sub: get the wrong end of the stick, spell it out, get your point across

L.p: In British English, you *get the wrong end of the stick* when you understand a situation or remark in completely the wrong way. Two people *get their wires crossed* when each one thinks the other meant something different. You *lose the thread* when you can no longer follow what someone is saying. If you *miss the point*, you fail to understand the most important part of something. An explanation that *goes over your head* is too difficult for you to understand.

L.e: I think you've got the wrong end of the stick – she's his sister, not his girlfriend. We got our wires crossed and waited at different cafés. The lecture was so long that I lost the thread halfway through. You've missed the point: the problem isn't the cost, it's the delay. Most of the jokes went over the children's heads.

L.x: Sorry, I *got the wrong end of the stick* (not *got the wrong side of the stick*).

L.p: You *spell it out* when you explain something in a very clear and simple way, often because someone has not understood. You *get your point across* when you make people understand what you mean. Something *in black and white* is written down, so it is clear and cannot be argued about. *In plain English* means in simple language that anyone can understand. You *drive the point home* when you say something firmly so that people fully understand it. If you hear someone *loud and clear*, you understand their message completely.

L.e: Do I have to spell it out? We can't afford a new car. She used pictures to get her point across. I want the agreement in black and white. The leaflet explains your rights in plain English. To drive the point home, the coach showed us a video of our mistakes. 'No phones at dinner.' 'Message received loud and clear.'

L.x: The rules are there *in black and white* (not *in white and black*).

L.h: C Keeping in touch and passing on news

L.p: You *drop someone a line* when you write them a short letter, email or message. If you *keep someone posted*, you keep giving them the latest news about something. In business English, you *touch base* with someone when you contact them briefly to share information. You *hear something on the grapevine* when you hear news unofficially, from people talking. In British English, *a word in your ear* is a quiet, private piece of advice or warning.

L.e: Drop us a line once you've settled in Sydney. I'll keep you posted about the house sale. Let's touch base again after the meeting. Apparently Sam is leaving – or so I heard on the grapevine. Can I have a word in your ear about the new manager?

L.x: I heard it *on the grapevine* (not *on the vine*) that they're getting married.

units.sub: every cloud has a silver lining, too many cooks spoil the broth, look before you leap

L.p: Proverbs are short, well-known sayings that give advice or state a general truth. *Every cloud has a silver lining* means that there is something good in every bad situation. *It's an ill wind* (that blows nobody any good) means that even a bad event helps somebody. *Where there's a will, there's a way* means that if you really want to do something, you will find a way. *Rome wasn't built in a day* means that important things take time. *Practice makes perfect* means that if you do something regularly, you become very good at it.

L.e: I lost my job, but every cloud has a silver lining – now I can retrain as a nurse. The rain ruined the fair, but the umbrella sellers did well. It's an ill wind. She had no money for university, but where there's a will, there's a way. Your Spanish will improve; Rome wasn't built in a day. I hated the piano at first, but practice makes perfect.

L.x: Every cloud has *a silver lining* (not *a golden lining*).

L.p: *Look before you leap* means think carefully about the possible results before you act. *Don't count your chickens* (before they're hatched) means do not be too sure of success before it actually happens. *Better safe than sorry* means it is wiser to be careful now than to have problems later. *Don't put all your eggs in one basket* means do not depend on just one plan, person or thing. *Prevention is better than cure* means it is easier to stop a problem happening than to fix it afterwards.

L.e: Read the contract carefully – look before you leap. They think they've won the contract, but I wouldn't count my chickens yet. Take an umbrella. Better safe than sorry. He invested in several companies so that he didn't put all his eggs in one basket. Get your boiler checked every year; prevention is better than cure.

L.x: Don't put all your eggs in *one basket* (not *one box*).

L.p: *Too many cooks spoil the broth* means that when too many people try to manage the same job, they do it badly. On the other hand, *many hands make light work* means that a job is easier when many people help. *Birds of a feather flock together* means that people with similar interests or characters spend time together. *The early bird catches the worm* means that people who act early get an advantage. *You can't teach an old dog new tricks* means that it is hard for people to change the way they do things. *When in Rome* (do as the Romans do) means that you should follow local customs when you are abroad.

L.e: Six people tried to plan the wedding, and it was chaos – too many cooks spoil the broth. If we all help to clear up, it won't take long. Many hands make light work. All his friends are keen cyclists, too; birds of a feather flock together. Get to the sale at nine. The early bird catches the worm. My dad refuses to use a smartphone – you can't teach an old dog new tricks. Everyone eats dinner at ten here, so we did the same. When in Rome!

L.x: Too many cooks spoil *the broth* (not *the soup*).

L.tip: People often say only the first part of a proverb, because everyone knows the rest: 'Don't count your chickens…', 'When in Rome…', 'It's an ill wind…'.

units.sub: on the tip of your tongue, ring a bell, a memory like a sieve

L.p: If a name or fact *rings a bell*, it seems familiar, although you cannot remember exactly why. You *jog someone's memory* when you say or show something that helps them remember. Memories *come flooding back* when you suddenly remember many things very clearly. Something that *sticks in your mind* is easy to remember for a long time. *A trip down memory lane* is a time when you enjoy remembering the past.

L.e: 'Do you know Ben Carter?' 'The name rings a bell.' Maybe this photo will jog your memory. When I walked into my old school, it all came flooding back. One thing her teacher said has always stuck in her mind. Looking through Grandma's letters was a real trip down memory lane.

L.x: Does the name *ring a bell* (not *ring the bell*)?

L.p: A word that is *on the tip of your tongue* is one you know but cannot quite remember at that moment. Informally, someone with *a memory like a sieve* forgets things very easily. If something *slips your mind*, you forget to do it or forget about it. You *draw a blank* when you try to remember something but cannot. When *your mind goes blank*, you suddenly cannot remember anything at all, often because you are nervous.

L.e: What's that actor called? His name's on the tip of my tongue. I've got a memory like a sieve – I've lost my keys again. Sorry I didn't call you back; it completely slipped my mind. I tried to think of her husband's name, but I drew a blank. In the exam my mind went blank.

L.x: That actor's name? It's *on the tip of my tongue* (not *at the end of my tongue*).

L.p: You *make a mental note* of something when you decide to remember it. You *refresh your memory* when you look at something again so that you remember it better. People say *if memory serves* (me right) when they think they remember something correctly but are not completely sure. Something that has not happened *in living memory* has not happened during the life of anyone alive now. An event *etched on your memory* is one you will never forget. Formally, you *commit something to memory* when you learn it so that you can remember it exactly.

L.e: I made a mental note to buy more coffee. Before the interview, read the job description again to refresh your memory. If memory serves, the hotel was next to the cathedral. It was the worst flood in living memory. The day my son was born is etched on my memory. Actors have to commit hundreds of lines to memory.

L.x: It was the hottest summer *in living memory* (not *in alive memory*).

units.sub: the good old days, in the long run, in the nick of time

L.p: Older people often talk about *the good old days*, a time in the past that they remember as better than the present. People say *in my day* when they compare the present with their own youth, often in a critical way. Something that is *a thing of the past* no longer exists or happens. A problem that is *ancient history* happened long ago and no longer matters. If a past disagreement is *water under the bridge*, it is finished and forgiven.

L.e: Grandad loves talking about the good old days, when sweets cost a penny. In my day, children walked to school on their own. With online banking, queues at the bank are becoming a thing of the past. Don't worry about that silly argument – it's ancient history now. We had our differences, but that's all water under the bridge.

L.x: It's all *water under the bridge* (not *water over the bridge*) now.

L.p: *In the long run* means over a long period of time, or in the end. A plan or product *in the pipeline* is being prepared and will appear soon. Something *just around the corner* will happen very soon. If something is *on the horizon*, it seems likely to happen in the future. When something is *only a matter of time*, it is certain to happen sooner or later.

L.e: Buying good shoes saves money in the long run. The company has several new games in the pipeline. With spring just around the corner, the garden centres are busy. There are big changes on the horizon for the car industry. It's only a matter of time before someone gets hurt on that road.

L.x: Solar panels will save you money *in the long run* (not *in the long time*).

L.p: You do something *in the nick of time* when you do it just before it is too late. Something done *at the eleventh hour* is done at the last possible moment. People say *better late than never* when it is better for something to happen late than not at all. Someone *ahead of their time* has ideas that are too modern for the period they live in. A person who is *behind the times* has old-fashioned ideas. You say it is *high time* someone did something when they should have done it already.

L.e: The firefighters arrived in the nick of time. The strike was called off at the eleventh hour. My brother finally passed his driving test at fifty – better late than never! As a designer, she was ahead of her time. My dad is a bit behind the times; he still pays for everything in cash. It's high time you tidied your room.

L.x: We caught the train *in the nick of time* (not *in the neck of time*).

L.tip: After *it's high time*, use a past tense, although the meaning is present or future: It's high time we went home.

units.sub: round the clock, once in a blue moon, against the clock

L.p: Work that goes on *round the clock* continues all day and all night. You work *against the clock* when you hurry to finish before a time limit. Something that runs *like clockwork* happens smoothly and exactly as planned. If you arrive somewhere at six *on the dot*, you arrive at exactly six. You *turn back the clock* when you return to the situation of an earlier time; people often say that you can't.

L.e: Nurses in the unit work round the clock. The builders were working against the clock to finish before winter. The whole wedding went like clockwork. The meeting starts at nine on the dot. I wish I could turn back the clock and choose a different university.

L.x: Please be here at ten *on the dot* (not *on the point*).

L.p: Something that happens *once in a blue moon* happens very rarely. *Every now and then* means sometimes, but not regularly. If you do something *day in, day out*, you do it every day for a long time, and it often becomes boring. Something that happens *on and off* happens sometimes, with breaks in between. Things that are *few and far between* are rare. *Nine times out of ten* means almost always.

L.e: My brother phones once in a blue moon. Every now and then we treat ourselves to a meal out. Day in, day out, he sits at the same desk. It has been raining on and off all week. Good plumbers are few and far between. Nine times out of ten, the bus is late.

L.x: We eat out *once in a blue moon* (not *one time in a blue moon*).

L.h: C Having time and losing it

L.p: If you are *pressed for time*, you do not have enough time. You *kill time* when you do something unimportant while you wait. Someone with *time on their hands* has free time and nothing special to do. You *make up for lost time* when you do a lot of something because you could not do it before. If you *buy time*, you find a way to delay something so that you have longer to act.

L.e: Sorry, I can't stop – I'm a bit pressed for time. We killed time at the airport by looking round the shops. Since he retired, he's had a lot of time on his hands. After years apart, the brothers are making up for lost time. The lawyer kept asking questions to buy time.

L.x: Since I retired, I've had plenty of *time on my hands* (not *time in my hands*).

units.sub: a storm in a teacup, add fuel to the fire, a breath of fresh air

L.p: You *add fuel to the fire* when you make an angry or difficult situation even worse. People say *there's no smoke without fire* when they think a rumour is probably partly true. A person or plan that *comes under fire* is strongly criticised. You *hold fire* when you wait before acting or criticising. If you go *out of the frying pan into the fire*, you escape from a bad situation into one that is even worse.

L.e: Shouting at him will only add fuel to the fire. Everyone says the manager is leaving, and there's no smoke without fire. The new tax has come under fire from small businesses. Let's hold fire until we have all the facts. I left a boring job for a stressful one – out of the frying pan into the fire!

L.x: His comments only *added fuel to the fire* (not *added oil to the fire*).

L.p: If you are *in deep water*, you are in serious trouble. You *test the water* when you try something in a small way to see how people react. If someone *pours cold water on* an idea, they criticise it so that people lose interest in it. Criticism that is *like water off a duck's back* has no effect on the person it is aimed at. You *make a splash* when you attract a lot of attention.

L.e: The company is in deep water after losing its biggest customer. Before opening a shop, she tested the water with a market stall. My parents poured cold water on my plan to travel for a year. I tell him to tidy up, but it's like water off a duck's back. The young designer made a splash at London Fashion Week.

L.p: In British English, *a storm in a teacup* is a lot of anger or worry about something unimportant. Someone or something that is *a breath of fresh air* is new, different and exciting. *The calm before the storm* is a quiet period before a time of trouble or activity. You *steal someone's thunder* when you take the attention or praise that they should have had. If something *takes the wind out of your sails*, it suddenly makes you less confident. Something that *vanishes into thin air* disappears completely.

L.e: The row about the parking spaces was just a storm in a teacup. The new head teacher has been a breath of fresh air. The office was quiet – the calm before the storm of the Christmas rush. I was going to announce my engagement, but my sister stole my thunder with hers. His criticism really took the wind out of my sails. My keys seem to have vanished into thin air.

L.x: The whole row was *a storm in a teacup* (not *a storm in a glass of water*).

units.sub: out of the blue, in the red, a white lie

L.p: If you are *in the red*, you owe money to the bank, and if a business is *in the black*, it is making a profit. *Red tape* is official rules and paperwork that cause delays. You *catch someone red-handed* when you find them in the act of doing something wrong. When people *roll out the red carpet*, they give a visitor a special welcome. In British English, *a red-letter day* is a very happy or important day that you will always remember.

L.e: My account is in the red again. After two difficult years, the shop is back in the black. Opening a café involves a lot of red tape. The thief was caught red-handed with the laptop under his arm. The town rolled out the red carpet for the Olympic champion. The day my first book came out was a red-letter day.

L.x: My bank account is *in the red* (not *in red*) again.

L.p: Something that happens *out of the blue* happens suddenly and unexpectedly. If you are *green with envy*, you are very jealous. You *give someone the green light* when you give them permission to start something. In British English, someone with *green fingers* is good at making plants grow. *A grey area* is a situation where the rules are not clear.

L.e: Out of the blue, an old friend called me from Canada. My friends were green with envy when they saw my new car. The council has given the green light to the new swimming pool. Look at those roses – you must have green fingers. Working from abroad is a grey area in many contracts.

L.x: When she saw my new flat, she was *green with envy* (not *yellow with envy*).

L.p: *A white lie* is a small lie that you tell to be polite or to avoid hurting someone. *A white elephant* is something that cost a lot of money but is useless. If you are *black and blue*, you are covered in bruises. *The black sheep* of a family is the member that the others think is bad or embarrassing. Someone *whiter than white* is completely honest and good, or pretends to be.

L.e: I told a white lie and said I loved the jumper. The new airport is a white elephant – hardly any planes use it. After falling off his bike, he was black and blue. My cousin is the black sheep of the family; he's always in trouble. The politician likes to appear whiter than white.

units.sub: a level playing field, the ball is in your court, below the belt

L.p: *A level playing field* is a situation in which everyone has the same chance of success. A remark that is *below the belt* is unfair and unkind, like an illegal punch in boxing. People *move the goalposts* when they change the rules or aims of something in a way that is unfair to others. In old-fashioned British English, behaviour that is *not cricket* is not fair or honest. If something is *par for the course*, it is normal and what you would expect, usually in a bad way.

L.e: Small shops want a level playing field with the online giants. Mentioning his divorce in the debate was a bit below the belt. Every time we finish the report, the boss moves the goalposts. Reading other people's letters just isn't cricket. Delays are par for the course on this railway line.

L.x: Whenever we get close, the managers *move the goalposts* (not *move the goals*).

L.p: When *the ball is in your court*, it is your turn to act or make a decision. You *get the ball rolling* when you start an activity, and other people then join in. If you *take your eye off the ball*, you stop giving attention to something important. *A whole new ball game* is a completely different situation that needs different skills. Something that is *out of your league* is too good or too expensive for you.

L.e: We've sent them our offer, so the ball is in their court now. Let me get the ball rolling by introducing myself. The team took their eye off the ball and lost in the last minute. Managing twenty people is a whole new ball game for her. A flat in that area is way out of our league.

L.x: I've made my offer, so *the ball is in your court* (not *the ball is on your field*).

L.p: Two competitors who are *neck and neck* are level, and either could win. You *win hands down* when you win very easily. If you are *in the running* for something, you have a chance of getting it. You *throw in the towel* when you stop trying because you know you cannot succeed. Someone who is *on the ropes* is close to defeat. You are *saved by the bell* when something ends a difficult situation just before you get into trouble.

L.e: The two parties are neck and neck in the polls. Our team won hands down. She's in the running for the head teacher's job. After three failed attempts, he threw in the towel. The company has been on the ropes since the scandal. The teacher was about to ask me a question when the fire alarm went off. Saved by the bell!

units.sub: a dark horse, an eager beaver, a cold fish

L.p: *An eager beaver* is a person who is very keen and works very hard, sometimes too hard. *A bookworm* loves reading. You are *a guinea pig* when people try out something new on you, such as a medicine or a teaching method. In British English, *a dogsbody* is someone who does all the boring jobs that nobody else wants to do. *A dark horse* is a person who keeps their talents secret, or a competitor that nobody expected to do well. *The underdog* is the person or team that everyone expects to lose.

L.e: The new trainee is a real eager beaver – she arrives before everyone else. As a child, I was a bookworm. Our class were guinea pigs for a new way of teaching maths. I'm just the office dogsbody: I make the tea and do the photocopying. Sam is a dark horse; I had no idea he could sing. Everyone loves to support the underdog.

L.x: Our class were *guinea pigs* (not *test mice*) for the new exam.

L.p: *A night owl* likes staying up late and is most active at night. *A party animal* loves going to parties and having fun. *A social butterfly* moves from one group of people to another at social events and has lots of friends. *A lone wolf* prefers to be alone or to work alone. Someone described as *a cold fish* is unfriendly and shows no feelings.

L.e: I'm a night owl – I do my best work after midnight. At university he was a real party animal. She's a social butterfly; she knows everyone at the club. The detective in the novel is a lone wolf who doesn't trust his colleagues. Her new boyfriend seemed a bit of a cold fish.

L.x: I'm *a night owl* (not *a night bird*), so I hate early meetings.

L.h: C People to watch out for

L.p: *A snake in the grass* is a person who pretends to be your friend but secretly works against you. People use *fat cat* to criticise rich and powerful business people who earn too much. *A road hog* is a selfish driver who does not let other people pass or who drives in the middle of the road. *A copycat* copies what other people do or say. *A loan shark* lends money to people and charges very high interest.

L.e: I trusted him, but he turned out to be a snake in the grass. The fat cats in the City got huge bonuses while workers lost their jobs. Some road hog in a van wouldn't let me overtake. Stop being such a copycat and wear your own clothes! Desperate for money, he borrowed from a loan shark.
