units.sub: let the cat out of the bag, a wild goose chase, the lion's share

L.p: You *let the cat out of the bag* when you tell people a secret, usually by accident. Information that comes *straight from the horse's mouth* comes directly from the person who knows most about it. *A little bird told me* is a playful way of saying that you have heard some news but will not reveal where it came from. *The elephant in the room* is an obvious problem that everyone knows about but nobody wants to mention. In British English, you *put the cat among the pigeons* when you say or do something that makes people upset or excited.

L.e: We were planning a surprise party, but my brother let the cat out of the bag. It must be true – I heard it straight from the horse's mouth. 'How did you know it was my birthday?' 'A little bird told me.' Nobody at the meeting mentioned the elephant in the room: the company is losing money. His decision to resign really put the cat among the pigeons.

L.x: Who *let the cat out of the bag* (not *let the dog out of the bag*)?

L.h: B Wasted effort and difficult jobs

L.p: *A wild goose chase* is a long search for something that you cannot find, often because it does not exist. In British English, you *flog a dead horse* when you waste effort on something that has no chance of success. A task that is *like herding cats* is very hard to organise because everyone wants to do something different. You *kill two birds with one stone* when you achieve two things with one action. Informally, if you *make a pig's ear of* something, you do it very badly.

L.e: The address was wrong, so it was a wild goose chase. Asking the council for a new park is flogging a dead horse. Organising a school trip is like herding cats. I'll visit my aunt when I go to the dentist and kill two birds with one stone. I tried to cut my own hair and made a real pig's ear of it.

L.x: The map was wrong, so the whole trip was *a wild goose chase* (not *a wild duck chase*).

L.p: *The lion's share* of something is the biggest part of it. An amount of money described as *chicken feed* is very small. If you are *in the doghouse*, someone is annoyed with you because of something you did. People say *hold your horses* to tell someone to wait or to slow down. You *open a can of worms* when you start dealing with something that causes lots of new problems. Something that could go on *until the cows come home* could continue for a very long time.

L.e: The eldest son got the lion's share of the money. For a company that size, a thousand pounds is chicken feed. I forgot our anniversary, so I'm in the doghouse. Hold your horses! We haven't agreed to anything yet. Asking about the missing money opened a real can of worms. You can argue until the cows come home, but I won't change my mind.

units.sub: stick to your guns, bury the hatchet, a shot in the dark

L.p: You *stick to your guns* when you refuse to change your opinion, even though others disagree. People who are *up in arms* are very angry and are protesting about something. You *cross swords with* someone when you argue with them. Someone *on the warpath* is angry and looking for a person to blame. You *fight a losing battle* when you keep trying to do something that will probably fail. When *the battle lines are drawn*, people take sides and get ready for a fight or argument.

L.e: Everyone laughed at her idea, but she stuck to her guns. Parents are up in arms about the school's new uniform rules. He has crossed swords with the referee many times. Watch out – the boss is on the warpath. I'm fighting a losing battle trying to keep the kitchen tidy. The battle lines are drawn between the two parties over the new tax.

L.x: Even when they laughed, she *stuck to her guns* (not *stuck to her weapons*).

L.p: You *bury the hatchet* when you agree to stop arguing and become friends again. If you *hold out an olive branch*, you do something to show that you want to end a disagreement. People *call a truce* when they agree to stop fighting or arguing for a time. You *wave the white flag* when you admit that you have lost and give up.

L.e: After years of silence, the two brothers finally buried the hatchet. She held out an olive branch by inviting her neighbour for coffee. The children called a truce for the length of the car journey. After two hours of arguing, I waved the white flag and agreed to go camping.

L.x: After the wedding, the two families *buried the hatchet* (not *buried the axe*).

L.p: *A shot in the dark* is a guess made with very little information. You *jump the gun* when you do something too early, before the right moment. *A parting shot* is an unkind remark that you make just as you leave. *A loose cannon* is a person who behaves in an unpredictable way that causes problems. You *shoot yourself in the foot* when you do or say something that harms your own chances. *A double-edged sword* is something that has both good and bad effects.

L.e: I had no idea of the answer – it was a shot in the dark. His parents jumped the gun and told everyone about the wedding before he'd even proposed. 'And your cooking is awful!' was her parting shot. The new minister is a loose cannon. By arriving late to the interview, he really shot himself in the foot. Fame can be a double-edged sword.

L.x: My answer was just *a shot in the dark* (not *a shoot in the dark*).

units.sub: a piece of cake, spill the beans, have your cake and eat it

L.p: Something that is *a piece of cake* is very easy to do. *A hard nut to crack* is a problem that is difficult to solve, or a person who is difficult to understand or persuade. In British English, if something is *not your cup of tea*, it is not the kind of thing you like. Products that *sell like hot cakes* sell very quickly. People humorously call a new invention *the best thing since sliced bread* when they think it is excellent.

L.e: Don't worry about the test – it'll be a piece of cake. The new manager is a hard nut to crack; nobody knows what she thinks. Opera isn't really my cup of tea. Tickets for the final sold like hot cakes. My dad thinks his new coffee machine is the best thing since sliced bread.

L.x: For her, the exam was *a piece of cake* (not *a piece of pie*).

L.p: You *spill the beans* when you tell people something that was meant to be secret. Something that gives you *food for thought* makes you think seriously about a subject. You *butter someone up* when you are very nice to them because you want something. If you are *walking on eggshells*, you are being very careful not to upset someone. You *have egg on your face* when you are embarrassed because something you said or did turned out to be wrong.

L.e: Come on, spill the beans – who's your new girlfriend? The documentary gave me a lot of food for thought. He's been buttering up his parents because he wants a car. Since their argument, we've all been walking on eggshells around him. The minister was left with egg on his face when the figures turned out to be wrong.

L.x: Come on, *spill the beans* (not *spill the peas*)!

L.p: Someone who wants to *have their cake and eat it* wants two good things that cannot both be possible. Your *bread and butter* is the work that gives you your main income. The person who *brings home the bacon* earns the money that a family lives on. In British English, plans that *go pear-shaped* go wrong. People say there's no use *crying over spilt milk* when it is pointless to be upset about something that has already happened. A *half-baked* idea has not been properly thought through.

L.e: You want a well-paid job with no stress? You can't have your cake and eat it. Weddings are our bread and butter, but we do birthday parties too. In their house, it's the wife who brings home the bacon. The holiday went pear-shaped when our flight was cancelled. The money's gone, and there's no use crying over spilt milk. His plan to sell ice cream in winter seems a bit half-baked.

L.x: The money has gone, so there's no use *crying over spilt milk* (not *crying over spilt water*).

L.tip: You can say that something is *as easy as pie*, but *a piece of pie* is not an idiom: the easy thing is *a piece of cake*.

units.sub: a dead end, at a crossroads, middle of the road

L.p: *A dead end* is a situation in which no more progress is possible. If you are *at a crossroads*, you have reached a point where you must make an important decision. *The end of the road* is the point where something cannot continue. *A fork in the road* is a point where you must choose between two different possibilities. *The light at the end of the tunnel* is a sign that a difficult period will soon end.

L.e: The police investigation has reached a dead end. At forty, she was at a crossroads in her career. After twenty years, this is the end of the road for the old factory. I'd reached a fork in the road: stay in London or move back home. After months of treatment, the light at the end of the tunnel is finally in sight.

L.x: After a long, hard winter, *the light at the end of the tunnel* (not *the light at the end of the road*) is in sight.

L.p: Music, ideas or politics that are *middle of the road* are moderate and ordinary, not extreme or exciting. If you are *on the right track*, you are doing something that will lead to success. People say they do not want to *go down that road* when they do not want to choose a particular course of action. A government *does a U-turn* when it completely changes its policy. Something that *paves the way for* something else makes it possible.

L.e: The band's music is very middle of the road. Your essay isn't finished, but you're on the right track. We could sue them, but I don't want to go down that road. The government has done a U-turn on school meals. The new law paved the way for women to vote.

L.x: Keep going – you're *on the right track* (not *on the right road*).

L.p: Informally, you *hit the road* when you leave a place or start a journey. Someone who lives *in the fast lane* has an exciting, busy life with lots of activity. You *put the brakes on* something when you slow it down or stop it. *A bumpy ride* is a difficult period with many problems. You *take a wrong turn* when you make a bad decision. In British English, something that *drives you round the bend* annoys you very much.

L.e: It's getting late – we'd better hit the road. After years in the fast lane, he moved to a quiet village. The bank has put the brakes on lending. The new airline has had a bumpy ride in its first year. Her life took a wrong turn when she left school at fifteen. The noise from next door drives me round the bend.

L.x: My neighbour's dog *drives me round the bend* (not *drives me round the corner*).

units.sub: on the house, go down the drain, under the same roof

L.p: In a bar or restaurant, food or drink *on the house* is free. People who live *under the same roof* share a home. *A roof over your head* is a place to live. In British English, something *as safe as houses* is very safe. Humorously, people who *eat you out of house and home* eat a lot of your food. A performer who *brings the house down* makes the audience laugh or clap very loudly.

L.e: The owner gave us a bottle of wine on the house. Three generations live under the same roof. Whatever happens, you'll always have a roof over your head. Gold is supposed to be as safe as houses. My teenage sons are eating me out of house and home. Her last song brought the house down.

L.x: The coffee was *on the house* (not *from the house*), so we left a big tip.

L.p: Something that happens *behind closed doors* happens in private, without the public knowing. When *the writing is on the wall*, there are clear signs that something bad is going to happen. *A skeleton in the cupboard* is an embarrassing secret from someone's past. You *show someone the door* when you make them leave, often from a job. Plans or rules that *go out of the window* are no longer used or followed.

L.e: The decision was made behind closed doors. When sales fell for the third year, the writing was on the wall. The journalist was sure the minister had a skeleton in the cupboard. After the scandal, the club showed the manager the door. Once the baby arrived, our routine went out of the window.

L.tip: British English says *a skeleton in the cupboard*; American English says *a skeleton in the closet*.

L.p: Money or effort that *goes down the drain* is wasted. People say it is *the pot calling the kettle black* when someone criticises another person for a fault that they have themselves. You *throw the baby out with the bathwater* when you get rid of something good while trying to get rid of something bad. *Everything but the kitchen sink* means far more things than are necessary. A brand or person that is *a household name* is known by almost everyone.

L.e: If the business fails, all our savings will go down the drain. He called me untidy – talk about the pot calling the kettle black! The course has problems, but cancelling it would be throwing the baby out with the bathwater. We only went away for a weekend, but she packed everything but the kitchen sink. Fifty years ago, the company was a household name.

L.x: He called me lazy – that's *the pot calling the kettle black* (not *the pan calling the kettle black*)!

units.sub: beat about the bush, nip in the bud, out of the woods

L.p: In British English, you *beat about the bush* when you avoid saying something directly. You *bark up the wrong tree* when you are wrong about the reason for something or about who is responsible. If you go *out on a limb*, you say or do something that other people do not support, which puts you in a risky position. A person or business that is *out of the woods* has got through the most difficult part of a problem. You *nip* a problem *in the bud* when you stop it at an early stage. *A late bloomer* is someone whose talents develop later than other people's.

L.e: Stop beating about the bush and tell me what's wrong. If you think I broke the window, you're barking up the wrong tree. She went out on a limb to defend her colleague. The patient is improving, but she's not out of the woods yet. Teachers try to nip bullying in the bud. He was a late bloomer who didn't start painting until he was sixty.

L.x: If you think I took it, you're *barking up the wrong tree* (not *barking at the wrong tree*).

L.tip: American English says *beat around the bush*; British English usually says *beat about the bush*.

L.p: Something that is *not a bed of roses* is not as easy or pleasant as people think. In British English, you *lead someone up the garden path* when you deceive them. *A thorn in your side* is someone or something that keeps causing you problems. Work that *bears fruit* produces good results. People say *the grass is always greener* (on the other side of the fence) when other people's lives always seem better than their own.

L.e: Running a restaurant is not a bed of roses. He led her up the garden path for years with promises of marriage. The noisy neighbours have been a thorn in our side for months. All our hard work finally bore fruit. You think city life is better, but the grass is always greener.

L.x: Being famous isn't *a bed of roses* (not *a bed of flowers*).

L.p: You *make a mountain out of a molehill* when you treat a small problem as if it were a serious one. You *hit rock bottom* when your situation becomes as bad as it can possibly be. Something that *goes downhill* gets worse and worse. *An uphill struggle* is something that is very difficult to achieve. Informally and rather unkindly, someone who is *over the hill* is too old to do something well.

L.e: It's only a scratch – don't make a mountain out of a molehill. After losing his job and his home, he hit rock bottom. The service in that restaurant has gone downhill. Learning Chinese at seventy was an uphill struggle. Some people think footballers are over the hill at thirty-five.

L.x: It's only a small mistake – don't *make a mountain out of a molehill* (not *make an elephant out of a fly*).

units.sub: in the same boat, rock the boat, plain sailing

L.p: People who are *in the same boat* are in the same difficult situation. You *rock the boat* when you cause problems by trying to change a situation that other people are happy with. If you *miss the boat*, you are too late to take an opportunity. In British English, you *push the boat out* when you spend a lot of money to celebrate something. Someone who has *burnt their boats* has taken a step that leaves no way back to the old life.

L.e: Nobody can afford a holiday this year – we're all in the same boat. The team is winning, so the coach doesn't want to rock the boat. House prices have gone up so much that I think I've missed the boat. For their silver wedding anniversary, they really pushed the boat out. By resigning before finding a new job, she burnt her boats.

L.x: Don't worry – we're all *in the same boat* (not *on the same boat*).

L.p: Something that is *plain sailing* is easy and free of problems. If things are *on an even keel*, they are calm and steady after a difficult time. You *take a different tack* when you try a different way of dealing with something. People say *all hands on deck* when everyone is needed to help. You *batten down the hatches* when you prepare for a difficult period. Informally, you *go overboard* when you do something too much or with too much enthusiasm.

L.e: Once we found the right builder, the rest was plain sailing. After a difficult year, the business is back on an even keel. Shouting didn't work, so I took a different tack and asked nicely. It's the busiest day of the year, so it's all hands on deck. With a recession coming, companies are battening down the hatches. Don't go overboard with presents this Christmas.

L.tip: British English says *plain sailing*; American English often says *smooth sailing*.

L.p: A manager who *runs a tight ship* organises things strictly and efficiently. If you are *left high and dry*, you are left in a difficult situation without any help. When *the tide has turned*, a situation has changed completely, usually for the better. You *make waves* when you cause trouble or attract attention by doing something new. Someone *on the crest of a wave* is very successful at the moment.

L.e: Our head teacher runs a tight ship. When the tour company went bust, hundreds of travellers were left high and dry. We lost the first three matches, but the tide has turned now. The young lawyer has been making waves in the profession. After her hit album, she's on the crest of a wave.

units.sub: run out of steam, on the same wavelength, blow a fuse

L.p: You *run out of steam* when you lose energy or enthusiasm and cannot continue. *Full steam ahead* means with as much energy and speed as possible. You *recharge your batteries* when you rest so that you have energy again. A person or team *firing on all cylinders* is working with full energy and effectiveness. If you are *running on empty*, you are continuing although you have no energy left.

L.e: The campaign started well but ran out of steam after a month. Now we have the money, it's full steam ahead with the new library. I'm going to the coast for a week to recharge my batteries. In the second half, the team was firing on all cylinders. After three nights with the baby, I'm running on empty.

L.p: People who are *on the same wavelength* understand each other well because they think in a similar way. People say *it's not rocket science* when something is not difficult to understand. *A cog in the machine* is a person who has a small, unimportant job in a large organisation. *A well-oiled machine* is an organisation or team that works smoothly. *The nuts and bolts* of something are its basic practical details. You *pull the plug* on a project when you stop it, usually by ending its money.

L.e: We've only just met, but we're on the same wavelength. Just follow the instructions – it's not rocket science. In a big company, it's easy to feel like a cog in the machine. The restaurant kitchen ran like a well-oiled machine. This course teaches the nuts and bolts of running a small business. The channel pulled the plug on the series after one season.

L.x: Don't panic – *it's not rocket science* (not *it's not a rocket science*).

L.p: Informally, you *blow a fuse* when you suddenly become very angry. A person with *a short fuse* gets angry very easily. In British English, something that *throws a spanner in the works* causes problems that stop a plan from working. A system that *goes into meltdown* stops working because there is too much pressure on it. An event that *sets off a chain reaction* causes a series of other events, each one causing the next.

L.e: When he saw the bill, my dad blew a fuse. Be careful what you say to her – she has a short fuse. We'd planned everything, but the train strike threw a spanner in the works. When the computers crashed, the airport went into meltdown. The bank's collapse set off a chain reaction across the world.

L.tip: British English says *a spanner in the works*; American English says *a wrench in the works*.

units.sub: rule of thumb, lend a hand, keep your fingers crossed

L.p: You *keep your fingers crossed* when you hope that something will happen. Someone who *has a finger in every pie* is involved in many different activities. In British English, if you are *all fingers and thumbs*, you are clumsy with your hands. You *point the finger at* someone when you blame them. If you *get your fingers burnt*, you suffer because of something risky that you tried. Informally and rather rudely, people tell someone to *pull their finger out* when they want them to start working harder.

L.e: I'm keeping my fingers crossed for sunshine tomorrow. My aunt has a finger in every pie in the village. I'm all fingers and thumbs today – that's the second cup I've broken. The report pointed the finger at the hospital managers. He got his fingers burnt on the stock market and won't invest again. Tell your brother to pull his finger out, or he'll fail the course.

L.x: I'm *all fingers and thumbs* (not *all hands and fingers*) this morning.

L.p: *A rule of thumb* is a practical way of judging or doing something that is not exact but is generally right. If you are *under someone's thumb*, they control you completely. You *give something the thumbs up* when you approve of it. Someone who *sticks out like a sore thumb* is very noticeable because they are different from everyone around them. You *twiddle your thumbs* when you have nothing to do while you wait.

L.e: As a rule of thumb, allow one hour of revision for every hour of lessons. He's completely under his mother's thumb. The council has given the plans the thumbs up. In my old jeans, I stuck out like a sore thumb at the party. The computers were down, so we sat twiddling our thumbs all morning.

L.x: As a *rule of thumb* (not *rule of finger*), allow an hour for every page.

L.p: You *lend a hand* when you help someone. A situation that *gets out of hand* becomes impossible to control. People say *my hands are tied* when rules stop them from doing what they would like to do. A house or business that *changes hands* is sold to a new owner. *First-hand* knowledge or experience comes from doing or seeing something yourself.

L.e: Could you lend a hand with these boxes? The party got out of hand and the police were called. I'd love to give you more time, but my hands are tied. The hotel has changed hands three times in ten years. She has first-hand experience of living in a war zone.

L.x: Could you *lend me a hand* (not *borrow me a hand*) with this table?

units.sub: put your foot down, drag your heels, on your toes

L.p: You *put your foot down* when you firmly refuse to allow something. In British English, you *put your foot in it* when you say something that upsets or embarrasses someone by accident. If you *get off on the wrong foot* with someone, your relationship starts badly. You *find your feet* when you become confident in a new place or job. People *get cold feet* when they suddenly become nervous about something they planned to do. You *foot the bill* when you pay for something, often something expensive.

L.e: When my son wanted a motorbike, I put my foot down. Asking about her husband was a mistake – I didn't know they'd separated, and I'd put my foot in it. We got off on the wrong foot, but now we're good friends. It took me a few months to find my feet at university. Two weeks before the wedding, he got cold feet. Taxpayers will have to foot the bill for the new stadium.

L.x: A week before the wedding, he *got cold feet* (not *got cold legs*).

L.p: You *drag your heels* when you do something slowly because you do not want to do it. If you *dig your heels in*, you refuse to change your mind, even when people put pressure on you. Someone who is *hot on your heels* is following very closely behind you. Your *Achilles' heel* is your weak point. In British English, you *kick your heels* when you have to wait with nothing to do.

L.e: The council has been dragging its heels over the new cycle lanes. I wanted to sell the car, but my wife dug her heels in. The police were hot on the thieves' heels. Spelling has always been my Achilles' heel. We kicked our heels at the airport for six hours.

L.x: Stop *dragging your heels* (not *pulling your heels*) and fill in the form.

L.p: If you are *on your toes*, you are alert and ready to deal with anything that happens. You *tread on someone's toes* when you upset them by getting involved in something that is their responsibility. *From head to toe* means over your whole body. In British English, something *toe-curling* is so embarrassing that it is uncomfortable to watch or listen to. You *dip a toe in the water* when you try something new in a small, careful way.

L.e: A good teacher keeps the class on their toes. I don't want to tread on anyone's toes, but I have an idea for the marketing campaign. The children came back from the field covered in mud from head to toe. His best man's speech was toe-curling. She dipped a toe in the water by selling her paintings online.

units.sub: a bone of contention, cost an arm and a leg, the cold shoulder

L.p: *A bone of contention* is a subject that people keep arguing about. If you *make no bones about* something, you say it openly and clearly, without feeling embarrassed. You *feel* something *in your bones* when you are sure about it although you have no proof. *The bare bones* of something are its most basic parts or facts. Something that is *bone dry* is completely dry.

L.e: Who does the washing-up has always been a bone of contention in our flat. She makes no bones about her ambition – she wants to run the company. We're going to win on Saturday – I just feel it in my bones. He told me the bare bones of the story, but not the details. After two months without rain, the garden is bone dry.

L.x: She *made no bones about* (not *made no bones of*) wanting the top job.

L.p: If someone *gives you the cold shoulder*, they treat you in a cold, unfriendly way on purpose, for example by not speaking to you. *A shoulder to cry on* is a person who listens kindly to your problems. You *rub shoulders with* famous or important people when you meet them and spend time with them. Someone with *a chip on their shoulder* is angry or resentful because they feel they have been treated unfairly in the past. People who stand *shoulder to shoulder* support each other and work together.

L.e: Since I forgot her birthday, my sister has been giving me the cold shoulder. When my marriage ended, my best friend was always a shoulder to cry on. As a journalist, she rubs shoulders with politicians and film stars. He's got a chip on his shoulder about not going to university. The whole village stood shoulder to shoulder against the new motorway.

L.p: Something that *costs an arm and a leg* is very expensive. Informally, you *twist someone's arm* when you persuade them to do something. If people welcome you *with open arms*, they are very pleased to see you. You *pull someone's leg* when you tell them something untrue as a joke. If you *don't have a leg to stand on*, you cannot prove what you say or defend what you did. A machine *on its last legs* is old and will soon stop working.

L.e: Their wedding must have cost an arm and a leg. 'Another piece of cake?' 'Well, if you twist my arm…' The refugees were welcomed with open arms. Don't believe him – he's pulling your leg. Without a receipt, I didn't have a leg to stand on. Our washing machine is on its last legs.

L.x: That watch must have *cost an arm and a leg* (not *cost a hand and a leg*).

units.sub: keep your head, off the top of your head, head over heels

L.p: You *keep your head* when you stay calm in a difficult situation, and you *lose your head* when you panic or cannot control your feelings. If you answer *off the top of your head*, you answer without checking the facts or thinking carefully. People *put their heads together* when they discuss a problem in order to solve it. In British English, if you *can't get your head round* something, you cannot understand it. Success that *goes to your head* makes you feel too proud of yourself.

L.e: When the fire alarm went off, the teacher kept her head. He lost his head and started shouting at the referee. Off the top of my head, I'd say there were about fifty people there. If we put our heads together, we'll find a solution. I can't get my head round these new tax rules. Don't let one good review go to your head.

L.x: I don't know the exact figure *off the top of my head* (not *from the top of my head*).

L.p: If you fall *head over heels* in love, you fall completely in love with someone. Informally, you *laugh your head off* when you laugh a lot. You *bite someone's head off* when you speak to them angrily for no good reason. If you are *banging your head against a brick wall*, you keep trying to do something but nothing changes. A person or thing that *turns heads* attracts attention because it is so attractive or unusual.

L.e: They met on holiday and fell head over heels in love. The film was so funny that we laughed our heads off. I only asked what time dinner was – there's no need to bite my head off! Trying to get the landlord to fix the heating is like banging your head against a brick wall. Her bright red car turns heads wherever she goes.

L.x: Within a week, they had fallen *head over heels* (not *heels over head*) in love.

L.p: You *keep your head down* when you avoid attracting attention and concentrate on your work. When people say *heads will roll*, they mean that people will be punished or lose their jobs because of a mistake. *A head start* is an advantage that you have over other people at the beginning of something. If you are *head-hunted*, another company asks you to come and work for them. You *hold your head up high* when you feel proud, not ashamed, of what you have done.

L.e: I'm new here, so I'm just keeping my head down. After the data was lost, everyone knew heads would roll. Children who are read to at home get a head start at school. She was head-hunted by a bank in Frankfurt. We lost the final, but we can hold our heads up high.

units.sub: keep a straight face, let your hair down, get off your chest

L.p: You *keep a straight face* when you manage not to laugh, although something is funny. You *lose face* when people stop respecting you, and you *save face* when you avoid this. You *put on a brave face* when you try to look happy or confident although you are upset. *A slap in the face* is an action that insults or upsets someone, especially when they did not expect it. *On the face of it* means judging by how something first appears.

L.e: When the vicar's trousers fell down, nobody could keep a straight face. The minister refused to apologise because he didn't want to lose face. The company called the job cuts 'restructuring' to save face. She put on a brave face at the funeral. Not being invited to the wedding was a real slap in the face. On the face of it, the offer looks good, but read the small print.

L.x: It was so funny that I couldn't *keep a straight face* (not *keep a serious face*).

L.p: You *let your hair down* when you relax and enjoy yourself, especially after working hard. People who *split hairs* argue about very small differences that are not important. If someone does *not turn a hair*, they stay completely calm in a frightening or shocking situation. You *tear your hair out* when you are extremely worried or frustrated. Informally, *a bad hair day* is a day when everything seems to go wrong.

L.e: After the exams, the students really let their hair down. Stop splitting hairs – 'nearly' and 'almost' mean the same thing here. The pilot landed the plane in the storm without turning a hair. I've been tearing my hair out trying to get the printer to work. I missed the bus and spilt coffee on my shirt – it's a bad hair day.

L.x: Stop *splitting hairs* (not *cutting hairs*) – the meaning is the same.

L.p: You *get something off your chest* when you talk about something that has been worrying you, and feel better afterwards. Someone who is *breathing down your neck* is watching everything you do, which makes you feel uncomfortable. If you are *up to your neck in* something, you are very involved in it, or you have too much of it. You *keep your cards close to your chest* when you do not tell other people about your plans. You *risk your neck* when you do something dangerous.

L.e: I've been wanting to get this off my chest for weeks: I'm leaving. I can't work with my manager breathing down my neck all day. We're up to our necks in paperwork. The coach is keeping his cards close to his chest about Saturday's team. The firefighter risked his neck to save the dog.

L.x: Thanks for listening – it's good to *get it off my chest* (not *get it out of my chest*).

units.sub: turn a blind eye, keep an eye on, see eye to eye

L.p: You *keep an eye on* someone or something when you watch them to make sure they are safe or that nothing goes wrong. You *keep an eye out for* something when you watch for it to appear. A person who seems to *have eyes in the back of their head* notices everything that happens around them. Someone who is *eagle-eyed* notices very small details. *A bird's-eye view* is a view of a place from high above it. People *in the public eye* are famous and often appear on television or in the newspapers.

L.e: Could you keep an eye on the children while I make a phone call? Keep an eye out for a petrol station. Our teacher seemed to have eyes in the back of her head. An eagle-eyed shop assistant spotted the fake banknote. From the top of the tower you get a bird's-eye view of the city. Life in the public eye can be very stressful.

L.x: Could you *keep an eye on* (not *keep your eyes at*) my bag for a minute?

L.p: People who *see eye to eye* agree with each other. You *turn a blind eye* to something wrong when you pretend not to notice it. If there is *more to it than meets the eye*, something is more complicated or interesting than it first seems. *An eye-opener* is an experience that surprises you and teaches you something new. You do something *with your eyes open* when you know about the possible problems before you start.

L.e: My brother and I don't always see eye to eye about politics. The manager turns a blind eye when staff arrive late. There's more to this case than meets the eye. Working in a hospital for a week was a real eye-opener. I took the job with my eyes open – I knew the hours would be long.

L.x: My parents and I don't always *see eye to eye* (not *see eyes to eyes*).

L.p: If you *have your eye on* something, you would like to buy it or have it. A person who is *the apple of your eye* is someone you love very much and are proud of. People say *your eyes are bigger than your stomach* when you take more food than you can eat. Informally, someone or something that is *a sight for sore eyes* is very welcome to see. You can see something *in your mind's eye* when you can imagine it or remember it clearly.

L.e: I've had my eye on that leather jacket for weeks. His youngest daughter is the apple of his eye. You'll never finish all that pasta – your eyes are bigger than your stomach. After a long walk in the rain, the pub was a sight for sore eyes. I can still see my grandmother's kitchen in my mind's eye.

L.x: Her grandson is *the apple of her eye* (not *the apple of her eyes*).

units.sub: all ears, bite your tongue, by the skin of your teeth

L.p: If you are *all ears*, you are listening eagerly to what someone is going to say. News that is *music to your ears* is very pleasant to hear. You *keep your ear to the ground* when you pay attention to what people are saying so that you know what is happening. People say *my ears are burning* when they think others have been talking about them.

L.e: Tell me about your date – I'm all ears. 'You can go home early today.' 'That's music to my ears!' Estate agents keep their ear to the ground for new properties. 'We were just talking about you.' 'I thought my ears were burning!'

L.x: Go on, tell me everything – I'm *all ears* (not *all ear*).

L.p: People say *my lips are sealed* when they promise to keep a secret. News that spreads *by word of mouth* passes from person to person in conversation, not through advertising. You *put your money where your mouth is* when you support what you say with action or money. A remark that is *tongue in cheek* is meant as a joke, not seriously. *A slip of the tongue* is a small mistake that you make when speaking. You *bite your tongue* when you stop yourself from saying what you really think.

L.e: I promise I won't say a word to Mum. My lips are sealed. The restaurant doesn't advertise; all its customers come by word of mouth. If you think the plan will work, put your money where your mouth is and invest in it. His review of the film was rather tongue in cheek. I called my teacher 'Mum' – it was just a slip of the tongue. I wanted to argue, but I bit my tongue.

L.x: I won't tell a soul – *my lips are sealed* (not *my mouth is sealed*).

L.p: If you manage something *by the skin of your teeth*, you only just succeed. You *get your teeth into* something when you start doing it with energy and enthusiasm. Someone who *lies through their teeth* tells lies without any shame. Humorously, someone who is *long in the tooth* is rather old. Informally, you *poke your nose into* something when you try to find out about things that are not your business. If you *turn your nose up at* something, you refuse it because you think it is not good enough for you.

L.e: We caught the last train by the skin of our teeth. She can't wait to get her teeth into her new project. Everyone could see the salesman was lying through his teeth. I'm getting a bit long in the tooth for all-night parties. Stop poking your nose into my private life! My son turns his nose up at anything green on his plate.

L.x: She passed her driving test *by the skin of her teeth* (not *by the skin of her tooth*).

units.sub: learn by heart, a heart of gold, set your heart on

L.p: You *learn* something *by heart* when you learn it so well that you can say it without looking. In British English, if you know something *off by heart*, you can say it perfectly from memory. You say something *from the bottom of your heart* when you mean it very sincerely. What someone is like *at heart* is what they are really like, under the surface. You *have a change of heart* when you change your opinion or decision.

L.e: We had to learn the poem by heart for homework. My son knows every football score off by heart. I'd like to thank you from the bottom of my heart. He seems tough, but at heart he's very shy. She was going to sell the house, but at the last minute she had a change of heart.

L.x: I learnt the whole song *by heart* (not *by my heart*).

L.p: Someone with *a heart of gold* is very kind and generous. Someone with *a heart of stone* shows no sympathy for other people. If *your heart is in the right place*, you mean well, even when you make mistakes. *A heart-to-heart* is a serious, honest conversation between two people, often about personal feelings. A *big-hearted* person is kind and generous.

L.e: Our neighbour has a heart of gold – she does all the shopping for the old man next door. You'd need a heart of stone not to cry at that film. He forgot to bring the cake, but his heart was in the right place. After the argument, my dad and I had a long heart-to-heart. Thanks to some big-hearted strangers, the family has a new home.

L.x: She may look strict, but she has *a heart of gold* (not *a golden heart*).

L.p: If you *set your heart on* something, you want it very much. *Your heart sinks* when you suddenly feel sad or disappointed. If *your heart is in your mouth*, you feel very nervous or frightened. If you *lose heart*, you become discouraged and stop hoping for success. Doing something *to your heart's content* means doing it for as long as you like, with nobody to stop you. A *half-hearted* effort is made without much enthusiasm.

L.e: She has set her heart on studying medicine. My heart sank when I saw the queue. My heart was in my mouth as I opened the exam results. Don't lose heart – you'll find a job soon. On holiday the children can swim to their heart's content. He made a half-hearted attempt to tidy his room.

L.x: When I saw the size of the bill, *my heart sank* (not *my heart sunk*).

units.sub: pick someone's brains, in cold blood, have the guts

L.p: You *pick someone's brains* when you ask someone who knows a lot about a subject for information or advice. You *rack your brains* when you think very hard to remember or solve something. In British English, *a brainwave* is a sudden clever idea. If you are *in two minds* about something, you cannot decide what to do. You *speak your mind* when you say exactly what you think. Informally, if you are *out of your mind* with worry, you are extremely worried.

L.e: Can I pick your brains about digital cameras? I racked my brains, but I couldn't remember his name. Then I had a brainwave: why not hold the party in the garden? I'm in two minds about whether to go to the reunion. My grandmother always speaks her mind. Where have you been? We've been out of our minds with worry!

L.x: I'm *in two minds* (not *in two heads*) about the new job.

L.p: A crime done *in cold blood* is done deliberately and without any feeling of pity. Something that *makes your blood boil* makes you extremely angry. *Blood is thicker than water* means that family relationships are stronger than other relationships. *New blood* means new people who bring new ideas and energy to a group. If something is *in your blood*, it is a natural part of you, often because others in your family have it too.

L.e: The victims were killed in cold blood. The way some people treat animals makes my blood boil. I disagree with my brother, but blood is thicker than water. The club needs some new blood on its committee. Her parents were both actors, so performing is in her blood.

L.x: Cruelty to animals *makes my blood boil* (not *makes my blood cook*).

L.p: Informally, you *have the guts* to do something when you are brave enough to do it. *A gut feeling* is a strong feeling that something is true, although you cannot explain why. If you *hate someone's guts*, you hate them very much. A person with *nerves of steel* stays calm in difficult or dangerous situations. You *lose your nerve* when you suddenly become too frightened to do something.

L.e: I didn't have the guts to tell him the truth. I had a gut feeling that something was wrong. Those two hate each other's guts. Bomb disposal experts need nerves of steel. I was going to jump, but at the last moment I lost my nerve.

units.sub: back to square one, behind someone's back, put your back into it

L.p: If you are *back to square one*, you have to start something again from the beginning because your first attempt failed. A company or person that goes *back to basics* returns to the simple, important things. People say *there's no going back* when a decision cannot be changed. You *take a step back* when you stop for a moment to think about a situation calmly. If you *have your back to the wall*, you are in a very difficult situation with few ways out.

L.e: The buyer pulled out, so we're back to square one with the house sale. After years of fancy menus, the restaurant has gone back to basics. Once you sign the contract, there's no going back. Let's take a step back and look at what went wrong. With three players injured, the team has its back to the wall.

L.x: The plan failed, so we're *back to square one* (not *back to square zero*).

L.p: You do something *behind someone's back* when you do it without them knowing, often unkindly. You *stab someone in the back* when you betray someone who trusted you. People tell you to *watch your back* when others may try to harm you. Informally, you tell someone to *get off your back* when you want them to stop criticising you or telling you what to do. *You scratch my back and I'll scratch yours* is said when two people agree to do favours for each other.

L.e: I found out they'd been laughing at me behind my back. My business partner stabbed me in the back and started his own company with our customers. It's a tough office – watch your back. I'll do my homework later, so get off my back! He'll vote for her plan if she supports his. You scratch my back and I'll scratch yours.

L.x: They were laughing at me *behind my back* (not *at my back*).

L.p: Informally, you *put your back into it* when you use a lot of physical effort. You *break the back of* a job when you finish the hardest or biggest part of it. If you *turn your back on* someone, you refuse to help them or you leave them. A plan that is *on the back burner* has been delayed because it is not a priority now. In British English, *the back of beyond* is a place that is very far from towns. *A back-seat driver* is a passenger who keeps giving the driver advice that they do not want.

L.e: If you put your back into it, you'll finish digging by lunchtime. We've broken the back of the decorating – there's only the hall left. He turned his back on his family when he became famous. The extension is on the back burner until we've saved more money. They bought a cottage in the back of beyond. My father is a terrible back-seat driver.

L.x: Come on, *put your back into it* (not *put your back on it*)!

units.sub: a long face, in the long run, to cut a long story short

L.p: You say *at long last* when something finally happens after a long wait. *Before long* means soon. Informally, people say *long time no see* when they meet someone they have not seen for a long time. *In the long run* means over a long period, when you look at the final result. If you are in something *for the long haul*, you are ready to continue for a long, difficult time. A change that was *a long time coming* happened much later than it should have.

L.e: At long last, the new bridge is open. Don't worry – you'll feel at home before long. 'Long time no see! How have you been?' Learning to cook will save you money in the long run. Rebuilding the town will take years; we're in it for the long haul. Her promotion was a long time coming.

L.x: Spring is here *at long last* (not *at last long*).

L.p: People say *to cut a long story short* when they want to give only the main facts of a story. *The long and the short of it* is the basic situation, without the details. A *long-winded* speech or explanation is too long and boring. A list *as long as your arm* is a very long one. In British English, *not by a long chalk* means not at all, or not nearly.

L.e: To cut a long story short, we missed the ferry and slept in the car. The long and the short of it is that we can't afford a new kitchen. The manager gave a long-winded speech about targets. My to-do list is as long as your arm. The match isn't over yet – not by a long chalk.

L.tip: British English says *to cut a long story short*; American English usually says *to make a long story short*.

L.p: Someone with *a long face* looks sad or disappointed. You *have come a long way* when you have made a lot of progress. Something that *goes a long way* is very useful or lasts a long time, and a person who will *go a long way* will be very successful. An event that is *a long way off* will not happen for a long time. A *long-lost* relative or friend is someone you have not seen for many years.

L.e: Why the long face? Has something happened? You've come a long way since your first piano lesson. A little kindness goes a long way. That young chef will go a long way. Retirement is still a long way off for me. At the wedding, I met a long-lost cousin from Australia.

L.x: You've *come a long way* (not *gone a long way*) since your first lesson.

units.sub: draw the line, toe the line, read between the lines

L.p: You *draw the line at* something when you refuse to do or accept it, although you accept other things. You *toe the line* when you obey the rules or do what people in authority tell you to do. If a person *crosses the line*, they go beyond what is acceptable, for example by being rude or unfair. People who *take a hard line* on something deal with it very strictly. If there is *a fine line between* two things, they are very similar and it is easy to go from one to the other.

L.e: I'll help you move house, but I draw the line at carrying the piano. Staff who don't toe the line soon lose their jobs. Teasing is fine, but those comments crossed the line. The school takes a hard line on bullying. There's a fine line between confidence and arrogance.

L.x: I don't mind cooking, but I *draw the line at* (not *draw the line on*) washing his socks.

L.tip: Be careful with the spelling: *toe the line*, as if you put your toes on a line – not *tow*.

L.p: You *read between the lines* when you understand what someone really means, although they do not say it directly. Something *along the lines of* something else is similar to it. If something is *in line with* a rule or plan, it follows it or agrees with it. To *sign on the dotted line* is to put your name on a contract and so make an agreement official. Something that happened *somewhere along the line* happened at some point during a process, although you do not know exactly when.

L.e: Her letter sounds cheerful, but if you read between the lines, she's lonely. He said something along the lines of 'I'll think about it'. Pay will rise in line with inflation. Once you sign on the dotted line, the house is yours. Somewhere along the line, the two friends stopped speaking.

L.p: If your job or reputation is *on the line*, you could lose it. People *in the firing line* are in a position where they are likely to be criticised or attacked. On the phone, people ask you to *hold the line* when they want you to wait. *The end of the line* is the point where something cannot continue any further. Your *line of work* is the kind of job you do. If you are *first in line* for something, you will be the first to get it.

L.e: With sales falling, the manager knows his job is on the line. Ministers are in the firing line over the rise in prices. Please hold the line while I put you through. After three defeats, it was the end of the line for the coach. 'What line of work are you in?' 'I'm a plumber.' As the oldest son, he's first in line to take over the farm.

units.sub: a hard act to follow, get your act together, actions speak louder than words

L.p: Someone who is *a hard act to follow* is so good that the next person will find it difficult to do as well. You *put on an act* when you pretend to have feelings that you do not really have. *A balancing act* is a situation in which you try to manage several different things at the same time. Informally, someone who *does a vanishing act* disappears, often when they are needed. If you are *caught in the act*, someone sees you doing something wrong.

L.e: Our last captain was brilliant – she'll be a hard act to follow. Don't be fooled by his smile; he's putting on an act for the cameras. Working and raising three children is a difficult balancing act. Whenever it's time to wash up, my brother does a vanishing act. The burglar was caught in the act by a neighbour.

L.x: The old manager was *a hard act to follow* (not *a hard act to copy*).

L.p: Informally, you *get your act together* when you start organising yourself better so that you can do something well. People *get in on the act* when they join an activity that someone else started, often to share in its success. You *swing into action* when you suddenly start doing something quickly and effectively. A machine or person that is *out of action* is not working or not able to take part. *Actions speak louder than words* means that what people do shows more about them than what they say.

L.e: If you want to pass, you'll have to get your act together. When the first café was a success, everyone wanted to get in on the act. As soon as the alarm rang, the staff swung into action. Our only lift has been out of action for a week. He says he loves her, but actions speak louder than words.

L.x: If you want that job, you'd better *get your act together* (not *get your acts together*).

L.p: *Where the action is* means the place where the most exciting or important things are happening. Informally, if you want *a piece of the action*, you want to be involved in something successful and share its profits. A place that is *a hive of activity* is full of people who are busy working. *A flurry of activity* is a short period when people are suddenly very busy. In legal language, *an act of God* is a natural event, such as a flood, that nobody can control. In British English, *action stations* is a call to get ready for something that is about to happen.

L.e: Young designers move to London because that's where the action is. When the town became popular, every hotel chain wanted a piece of the action. The kitchen was a hive of activity before the wedding. The news caused a flurry of activity on the stock market. The insurance didn't cover the damage because it was an act of God. The guests arrive in ten minutes – action stations!

L.x: Before the party, the kitchen was *a hive of activity* (not *a nest of activity*).

units.sub: for good, too good to be true, go from bad to worse

L.p: If something happens *for good*, it happens permanently. Something *too good to be true* seems so good that you suspect there is a problem with it. An object that is *as good as new* is in excellent condition again after being repaired or cleaned. In British English, a child who is *as good as gold* behaves very well. You do something *for someone's own good* when it will help them, even if they do not like it. *Too much of a good thing* is an amount of something pleasant that is so large that it becomes unpleasant.

L.e: She's left her home town for good. A free holiday? It sounds too good to be true. After the repair, my bike is as good as new. The children were as good as gold all afternoon. I'm taking your phone away for your own good. I love chocolate, but you can have too much of a good thing.

L.x: She has left the country *for good* (not *for the good*).

L.p: Things that *go from bad to worse* get even worse than they already were. You *go through a bad patch* when you have a difficult period in your life or work. If you do something *with bad grace*, you do it unwillingly and in an unfriendly way. In old-fashioned British English, *a bad egg* is a dishonest or unpleasant person. In British English, *not bad* often means quite good, or even very good.

L.e: First the car broke down, then it started to rain – things went from bad to worse. Their marriage went through a bad patch, but they're happy now. He apologised, but with very bad grace. Don't lend him money; he's a bad egg. 'How was your holiday?' 'Not bad at all!'

L.x: After the storm, things went *from bad to worse* (not *from bad to worst*).

L.h: C Good and bad in relationships

L.p: In British English, if you are *in someone's good books*, they are pleased with you, and if you are *in someone's bad books*, they are annoyed with you. People say *good riddance* when they are glad that someone or something unpleasant has gone. You do something *in good faith* when you do it honestly, believing it is right. Someone who *makes good* becomes successful after a difficult start.

L.e: I cooked dinner, so I'm in my wife's good books. I forgot to call my mum, so I'm in her bad books. 'The noisy neighbours have moved out.' 'Good riddance!' I bought the car in good faith; I didn't know it was stolen. He grew up in poverty but made good as a businessman.

units.sub: break new ground, stand your ground, get off the ground

L.p: You *break new ground* when you do something that nobody has done before. A plan or business that *gets off the ground* starts successfully. An idea or group that is *gaining ground* is becoming more popular or successful, while one that is *losing ground* is becoming less popular. You *cover a lot of ground* when you deal with many subjects, or travel a long way. *The ground rules* are the basic rules that people agree to follow in an activity.

L.e: The film broke new ground in the use of special effects. Without more money, the project will never get off the ground. The idea of a four-day week is gaining ground. The party has lost ground in the polls. We covered a lot of ground in today's meeting. Before the debate, the teacher set out the ground rules.

L.x: Without investors, the project never *got off the ground* (not *got up the ground*).

L.p: You *stand your ground* when you refuse to change your opinion or move back, even when people attack you. *Common ground* is the opinions and interests that two people or groups share. If you are *on shaky ground*, your argument or position is weak and might not be right. *The middle ground* is a position between two opposite opinions. You are *on safe ground* when you are dealing with a subject you know well, where you are unlikely to make mistakes.

L.e: The protesters stood their ground when the police arrived. My father and I disagree about politics, but we find common ground on football. Without any evidence, you're on shaky ground. Most voters are somewhere in the middle ground. I'm on safe ground when we talk about cooking.

L.x: We disagree about most things, but we found some *common ground* (not *common floor*).

L.p: In British English, something that *suits you down to the ground* is perfect for you. People who *keep their feet on the ground* stay sensible and realistic, even when they are successful. People say they *wished the ground would swallow them up* when they felt terribly embarrassed. If you *run yourself into the ground*, you work so hard that you become exhausted. In British English, a person who *goes to ground* hides somewhere, usually to avoid people or trouble.

L.e: A job working outdoors would suit him down to the ground. Despite her fame, she has kept her feet on the ground. When I fell over on stage, I wished the ground would swallow me up. You're running yourself into the ground – take a holiday. After the scandal, the singer went to ground for months.

units.sub: as fit as a fiddle, like a fish out of water, sleep like a log

L.p: Similes compare two things using *as … as* or *like*. Someone *as fit as a fiddle* is very healthy. Something *as light as a feather* weighs very little. Humorously, something *as old as the hills* is very old. A person who is *as quiet as a mouse* makes almost no noise. Someone *as hard as nails* is tough and shows little sympathy. Humorously, an explanation that is *as clear as mud* is not clear at all.

L.e: My grandmother is ninety but as fit as a fiddle. This new laptop is as light as a feather. That joke is as old as the hills. The children were as quiet as mice during the film. The new manager is as hard as nails. 'Did you understand the instructions?' 'They were as clear as mud!'

L.x: Grandad is eighty-five but *as fit as a fiddle* (not *as fit as a violin*).

L.p: If you feel *like a fish out of water*, you feel uncomfortable because you are in a situation that is new or strange to you. Someone *like a bull in a china shop* is clumsy or careless, and often breaks things or upsets people. People who rush around *like headless chickens* are busy in a panicky, disorganised way. In British English, someone *like a bear with a sore head* is in a very bad mood. Someone *like a kid in a sweet shop* is very excited because they are surrounded by things they love.

L.e: At the fashion show, I felt like a fish out of water. He went into the meeting like a bull in a china shop and offended everyone. The day before the deadline, we were all running around like headless chickens. Dad's like a bear with a sore head until he's had his coffee. In the bookshop, she was like a kid in a sweet shop.

L.x: At the posh dinner, I felt *like a fish out of water* (not *like a fish out of the sea*).

L.p: You *sleep like a log* when you sleep very well and deeply. Someone who *eats like a horse* eats a lot. Clothes that *fit like a glove* fit perfectly. In British English, two people who are *like chalk and cheese* are completely different from each other. Something that is *like a red rag to a bull* is sure to make a particular person very angry.

L.e: After the long walk, I slept like a log. Teenage boys eat like horses. The dress fits like a glove. My two sisters are like chalk and cheese. Mentioning politics to my uncle is like a red rag to a bull.

L.x: The twins look alike, but in character they're *like chalk and cheese* (not *like chalk and butter*).

L.tip: In informal speech, the first *as* in a simile is often left out: *She's fit as a fiddle.*
